hits.title: Hierarchical Continuous Diffusion Language Models
hits.authors: Hui Ren, Zihan Li, Chang Liu, Huidong Liu, Alexander Schwing
hits.abstract: Discrete diffusion language models offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive generation for tasks demanding bidirectional reasoning and global constraint satisfaction. Yet they share a structural bottleneck: when decoding in parallel, each token is sampled independently from its marginal, severing the statistical dependencies among the tokens decoded together. Continuous diffusion language models avoid this by denoising a shared continuous state, but their denoiser sees only that state, so nothing ties it to a valid token configuration until it is finally decoded. To address this, we propose Hierarchical Continuous Diffusion Language Models (HC-DLM), which couple discrete token generation with a continuous latent trajectory in a single, principled denoising process, whose training objective is derived from a variational bound on the token likelihood. In contrast to recent methods that attach continuous context to a self-contained discrete chain, HC-DLM makes the latent the only persistent generative state: tokens are read out from it at every step and feed back as a scaffold for the next latent update. On structured reasoning (Sudoku), mathematical planning (Countdown) and language modeling (LM1B), HC-DLM improves over discrete and continuous diffusion baselines at matched model size, in puzzle accuracy on Sudoku and Countdown and in generative perplexity on LM1B. Project page: https://hc-dlm.github.io/.

Section: C EXTENDED COMPARISON WITH HYBRID DISCRETE-CONTINUOUS DIFFUSION

This section expands the comparison of Section 5 with three representative hybrid models that attach the continuous state to a discrete chain in different ways, namely a global latent drawn once (VMD), per-token hints (CADD), and a parallel embedding chain (CCDD). Table 10 summarizes the structural differences, and the paragraphs below give the details.

Section: C.4 SUMMARY

HC-DLM differs from all three hybrids in the last two columns of Table 10. Its token predictor reads only the latent, so every token is re-read from the latent at each step instead of being carried over once decoded. This suits the uniform kernel, which in our experiments works clearly better than the absorbing one (Table 5).

Table 7 reports the generative perplexity and entropy across different numbers of neural function evaluations (NFEs). Both metrics are computed over 1,024 unconditional samples at each NFE.

Section: B.6 INFERENCE SPEED

Figure 4 compares wall-clock sampling time per batch for HC-DLM and LangFlow under the same sampling budget and sequence length on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU. At larger batch sizes, HC-DLM maintains a lower time per batch than LangFlow, suggesting favorable efficiency for batched parallel generation.

Hierarchical Continuous Diffusion Language Models

Abstract: Discrete diffusion language models offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive generation for tasks demanding bidirectional reasoning and global constraint satisfaction. Yet they share a structural bottleneck: when decoding in parallel, each token is sampled independently from its marginal, severing the statistical dependencies among the tokens decoded together. On structured reasoning (Sudoku), mathematical planning (Countdown) and language modeling (LM1B), HC-DLM improves over discrete and continuous diffusion baselines at matched model size, in puzzle accuracy on Sudoku and Countdown and in generative perplexity on LM1B. Project page: https://hc-dlm.github.io/.

Section: 1 INTRODUCTION

Autoregressive (AR) language models generate text left-to-right. This sequential factorization is remarkably successful, yet it is a mismatch for tasks that need global constraint satisfaction or bidirectional computation, such as solving logical puzzles or planning arithmetic operations. On these tasks, AR models commit early to choices that are challenging to revise (Ye et al., 2025).
Discrete diffusion language models (Austin et al., 2021; Lou et al., 2024; Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025) provide a principled alternative. By modeling the joint distribution over all tokens via an iterative denoising process, they enable the model to condition on arbitrary subsets of tokens and refine its predictions over many bidirectional passes, decoding multiple tokens in parallel at each step. This yields empirical gains on reasoning and planning (Ye et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025) and, at scale, perplexity competitive with strong AR baselines (Nie et al., 2025; Lou et al., 2024).
However, a bottleneck remains at the heart of parallel decoding: token dependence. When the model unmasks multiple positions in a single denoising step, each position is independently sampled from its marginal conditioned on a partial sequence. Hence, the joint over the simultaneously decoded tokens is modeled as a product of marginals (Gu et al., 2018; Li et al., 2026; Hersche et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Ringel et al., 2026), which fails precisely where tokens are tightly coupled by syntax, logic, or physical constraints.
Continuous diffusion language models address this by denoising a continuous state shared by all tokens: tokens decoded in parallel all depend on the same latent instead of being sampled on their own. They denoise either the token embeddings (Li et al., 2022; Gulrajani & Hashimoto, 2023; Chen et al., 2026) or a compressed latent produced by an encoder (Zhang et al., 2023; Lovelace et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2026), and decode tokens from the clean result. Their weakness mirrors the discrete one. Their denoiser takes only the continuous state as input, and no term of the objective involves tokens along the trajectory, removing ties to a valid token configuration until the final decoding step.
1
Figure 1: HC-DLM coupled diffusion process. The forward direction independently corrupts the continuous latent trajectory x0 → xT and the discrete token trajectory k0 → kT via q(xt | xt − 1 ) and q(kt | kt − 1 ). The reverse direction couples the two channels: pϕ(xt − 1 | xt, kt) advances the continuous state conditioned on the current token state, while pθ(kt | xt) reads token distributions from the latent state, iterating until the clean states (x0, k0) are reached.
Latent Space
Rounding (Li et al., 2022) and self-conditioning (Chen et al., 2023; 2026) feed the model's own token estimate back as an input, but they share the same problem, since that estimate is neither a variable of the model nor a term of its objective.
The two weaknesses are complementary, and so are their remedies. Tokens decoded in parallel need a shared state to depend on, which a continuous latent provides, and a latent being denoised needs a discrete configuration to be tied to, which the tokens provide. We therefore propose Hierarchical Continuous Diffusion Language Models (HC-DLM), a generative framework whose reverse process is a two-level chain (Fig. 1). The continuous latent trajectory {xt} is the only state that persists across steps. At every reverse step, tokens are read out from the current latent through a readout distribution pθ(kt | xt), re-noised through the discrete forward kernel, and fed back as the condition of the next latent transition pϕ(xt − 1 | xt, kt). The token state is thus a variable of the generative model with a forward kernel of its own, which is what separates the scaffold from a fed-back estimate. In the generative model, kt depends on the past only through xt, so the tokens carry no transition chain of their own and every position is read out anew at each step. We call this organization the hierarchical coupling. It determines both how the model is trained and how it samples: a single variational bound over the two-level trajectory gives the training objective (Section 3.2), and generation alternates latent denoising with token readout and re-noising (Section 3.4).
Hybrid discrete–continuous diffusion models also pair the two spaces, through per-token continuous hints (CADD) (Zheng et al., 2026), or an embedding chain denoised in parallel with the tokens (CCDD) (Zhou et al., 2026). However, separate transition chains are used as discussed in Section 5 and Appendix C.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion language models offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive generation for tasks demanding bidirectional reasoning and global constraint satisfaction. Yet they share a structural bottleneck: when decoding in parallel, each token is sampled independently from its marginal, severing the statistical dependencies among the tokens decoded together. Continuous diffusion language models avoid this by denoising a shared continuous state, but their denoiser sees only that state, so nothing ties it to a valid token configuration until it is finally decoded. To address this, we propose Hierarchical Continuous Diffusion Language Models (HC-DLM), which couple discrete token generation with a continuous latent trajectory in a single, principled denoising process, whose training objective is derived from a variational bound on the token likelihood. On structured reasoning (Sudoku), mathematical planning (Countdown) and language modeling (LM1B), HC-DLM improves over discrete and continuous diffusion baselines at matched model size, in puzzle accuracy on Sudoku and Countdown and in generative perplexity on LM1B. Project page: https://hc-dlm.github.io/.

Section: Contributions.

Framework. We introduce HC-DLM (Section 3.1), a hierarchical generative structure for discrete sequences, in which a continuous latent is the only persistent state and tokens are per-step readouts that feed back as a conditioning scaffold.
A likelihood bound for the hierarchical coupling chain. We derive a variational lower bound for HC-DLM (Section 3.2) over the hierarchical trajectory, which establishes that reading tokens from the latent and feeding them back is a proper generative model of the token sequence.
Both the continuous latent and the token feedback are needed. We show on Sudoku, Countdown and LM1B that HC-DLM improves over discrete and continuous diffusion baselines at matched model size (Section 4), and that removing either one leaves a model that falls well short of the full one (Section 4.5).

Section: 2 PRELIMINARIES

Discrete Diffusion Models. A discrete diffusion language model (Austin et al., 2021; Sahoo et al., 2024) defines a forward Markov chain that progressively corrupts a discrete length L token sequence k 0 = (. . . , k i 0
, . . . ) ∈ V L over vocabulary V (|V| = K) with i ∈ {1, . . . , L}. Using a noise schedule α0 = 1 ≥ α1 ≥ · · · ≥ αT ≈ 0, the marginal at time t ∈ {0, . . . , T} interpolates between sequence

Following Austin et al. (2021), two common choices of π recover the standard discrete diffusion formulations: (i) absorbing (MASK) state , π (k) = δ(k − [MASK]), which corrupts each token toward a special mask symbol and underlies most masked diffusion language models (Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025); (ii) uniform state , π (k) = 1/K, which replaces tokens by a uniform draw over the vocabulary. A parametric model pθ(k0 | kt), typically a bidirectional transformer trained with token-level cross-entropy, reverses this corruption.
Token independence. During inference, the factored form pθ(k0 | kt) = Q i pθ(k i 0 | kt) samples each token independently. While the shared context kt provides some global information, the joint distribution over simultaneously decoded tokens is modeled as a product of marginals which does not capture their statistical dependencies.
Continuous Diffusion Models. For continuous data x 0 ∈ R d , a DDPM (Ho et al., 2020) defines a Gaussian forward process with tractable posterior q(xt − 1 | xt, x0) and trains a denoiser via a weighted MSE objective. Flow Matching (FM) (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023) takes a more direct approach, training a velocity network vϕ to regress a target vector field transporting noise ϵ ∼ N (0, I) to data x0. Using the affine interpolation xt = (1 − t) x0 + t ϵ, the Conditional Flow Matching objective is: LCFM = Et, x 0, ϵ -

Section: 3 HIERARCHICAL CONTINUOUS DIFFUSION LANGUAGE MODELS

In this section, we first define a coupled continuous–discrete trajectory whose forward corruption remains tractable while its reverse dynamics are organized into two levels, with tokens read out from the latent state and fed back as a scaffold for the next latent update. We then derive a variational lower bound for this hierarchical process, convert it into a practical training objective (Fig. 2), and describe the resulting alternating sampler.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion language models offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive generation for tasks demanding bidirectional reasoning and global constraint satisfaction. Section: 3.1 GENERATIVE MODEL AND FORWARD PROCESS

The token-independence bottleneck calls for a reverse process whose state carries cross-token information before any token is final, and the weakness of latent diffusion calls for that state to stay anchored to a token sequence while it is denoised. We therefore make the continuous representation itself a denoising trajectory and let every reverse step update both the continuous state and the token scaffold that conditions it.
For this, we model a sequence of discrete tokens k0 ∈ V L by introducing a coupled continuous latent state x0 ∈ R M×d . M is the latent sequence length and d is the per-position embedding dimension. The model maintains two trajectories, a continuous one {xt} T t=0 and a discrete one {kt} T t=0 , that are corrupted independently in the forward direction but tightly coupled in the reverse direction.

The only learned component is the encoder qψ(x0 | k0), which produces a continuous latent representation of the clean token sequence. Jointly training it with the generative model permits the latent geometry to adapt to the needs of denoising. The continuous noising q(xt | xt − 1 ) is a standard Gaussian diffusion process with tractable marginals q(xt | x0) and closed-form posteriors q(xt − 1 | xt, x0). It converges to a standard Gaussian prior q(xT | x0)≈N (0, I) at the terminal time. For the discrete noising kernel q(kt | kt − 1 ) we use the categorical forward process defined in Eq. (1), with either an absorbing or uniform state distribution. Note that the two forward chains in Eq. (2) are independent: xt is corrupted by Gaussian noise while kt is corrupted separately by token-level noise.

The token-conditioned denoiser d ϕ (xt, kt, t/T) produces the clean-latent estimate xˆ ˆ 0 (loss Jcont), the token predictor pθ(k0 | x0) decodes x0 to ˆ k 0 (loss Jr Jrecon ), and the encoder is regularized by Jent .

This independence keeps both forward marginals tractable, exactly as in standard continuous and discrete diffusion.
Generative model (reverse process). While the forward chains are independent, the reverse chain deliberately breaks this symmetry: a continuous denoiser pϕ(xt − 1 | xt, kt) conditions on the current token state. Hence, information flows from discrete variables into the continuous trajectory at every step. Specifically, the joint generative model factorizes as follows:
Two learned distributions drive the reverse direction of Fig. 1. The token predictor pθ(kt | xt), with parameters θ, maps the noisy continuous state to a distribution over tokens at time t: at t=0 it produces the final discrete output, while at intermediate t it acts as a soft readout that maps the continuous state back to a distribution over the discrete vocabulary. The continuous denoiser pϕ(xt − 1 | xt, kt) , with parameters ϕ, advances the latent state conditioned on the current token state. Importantly, dependence of the denoising on kt makes HC-DLM more than two parallel diffusion processes: the token state acts as a discrete scaffold that resolves continuous-space ambiguity. Confident token estimates constrain the directions in which x t can move, while uncertain positions leave the continuous state free to explore alternative completions.
This intuition can be made precise. This reverse chain is a hierarchy rather than a pair of sibling processes, that is, two self-contained chains coupled at the same level. The token state has no transition kernel of its own: in Eq. (3), kt depends on the past only through xt, so all cross-step information travels through the continuous trajectory, and tokens are read out anew at every step, which keeps them revisable.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion language models offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive generation for tasks demanding bidirectional reasoning and global constraint satisfaction. Yet they share a structural bottleneck: when decoding in parallel, each token is sampled independently from its marginal, severing the statistical dependencies among the tokens decoded together. Section: 2 PRELIMINARIES

Discrete Diffusion Models. A discrete diffusion language model (Austin et al., 2021; Sahoo et al., 2024) defines a forward Markov chain that progressively corrupts a discrete length L token sequence k 0 = (. . . , k i 0
, . . . ) ∈ V L over vocabulary V (|V| = K) with i ∈ {1, . . . , L}. Using a noise schedule α0 = 1 ≥ α1 ≥ · · · ≥ αT ≈ 0, the marginal at time t ∈ {0, . . . , T} interpolates between sequence

Following Austin et al. (2021), two common choices of π recover the standard discrete diffusion formulations: (i) absorbing (MASK) state , π (k) = δ(k − [MASK]), which corrupts each token toward a special mask symbol and underlies most masked diffusion language models (Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025); (ii) uniform state , π (k) = 1/K, which replaces tokens by a uniform draw over the vocabulary. A parametric model pθ(k0 | kt), typically a bidirectional transformer trained with token-level cross-entropy, reverses this corruption.
Token independence. During inference, the factored form pθ(k0 | kt) = Q i pθ(k i 0 | kt) samples each token independently. While the shared context kt provides some global information, the joint distribution over simultaneously decoded tokens is modeled as a product of marginals which does not capture their statistical dependencies.
Continuous Diffusion Models. For continuous data x 0 ∈ R d , a DDPM (Ho et al., 2020) defines a Gaussian forward process with tractable posterior q(xt − 1 | xt, x0) and trains a denoiser via a weighted MSE objective. Flow Matching (FM) (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023) takes a more direct approach, training a velocity network vϕ to regress a target vector field transporting noise ϵ ∼ N (0, I) to data x0. Using the affine interpolation xt = (1 − t) x0 + t ϵ, the Conditional Flow Matching objective is: LCFM = Et, x 0, ϵ -
∥vϕ(xt, t) − (ϵ − x0)∥ 2  . Samples are generated by integrating x˙ ˙ = v ϕ (x, t) backward from t = 1 to t = 0, often with fewer function evaluations than DDPM sampling.

HC-DLM differs from all three hybrids in the last two columns of Table 10. Section: 1 INTRODUCTION

Autoregressive (AR) language models generate text left-to-right. This sequential factorization is remarkably successful, yet it is a mismatch for tasks that need global constraint satisfaction or bidirectional computation, such as solving logical puzzles or planning arithmetic operations. On these tasks, AR models commit early to choices that are challenging to revise (Ye et al., 2025).
Discrete diffusion language models (Austin et al., 2021; Lou et al., 2024; Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025) provide a principled alternative. By modeling the joint distribution over all tokens via an iterative denoising process, they enable the model to condition on arbitrary subsets of tokens and refine its predictions over many bidirectional passes, decoding multiple tokens in parallel at each step. This yields empirical gains on reasoning and planning (Ye et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025) and, at scale, perplexity competitive with strong AR baselines (Nie et al., 2025; Lou et al., 2024).
However, a bottleneck remains at the heart of parallel decoding: token dependence. When the model unmasks multiple positions in a single denoising step, each position is independently sampled from its marginal conditioned on a partial sequence. Hence, the joint over the simultaneously decoded tokens is modeled as a product of marginals (Gu et al., 2018; Li et al., 2026; Hersche et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Ringel et al., 2026), which fails precisely where tokens are tightly coupled by syntax, logic, or physical constraints.
Continuous diffusion language models address this by denoising a continuous state shared by all tokens: tokens decoded in parallel all depend on the same latent instead of being sampled on their own. They denoise either the token embeddings (Li et al., 2022; Gulrajani & Hashimoto, 2023; Chen et al., 2026) or a compressed latent produced by an encoder (Zhang et al., 2023; Lovelace et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2026), and decode tokens from the clean result. Their weakness mirrors the discrete one. Their denoiser takes only the continuous state as input, and no term of the objective involves tokens along the trajectory, removing ties to a valid token configuration until the final decoding step.
1
Figure 1: HC-DLM coupled diffusion process. The forward direction independently corrupts the continuous latent trajectory x0 → xT and the discrete token trajectory k0 → kT via q(xt | xt − 1 ) and q(kt | kt − 1 ). The reverse direction couples the two channels: pϕ(xt − 1 | xt, kt) advances the continuous state conditioned on the current token state, while pθ(kt | xt) reads token distributions from the latent state, iterating until the clean states (x0, k0) are reached.
Latent Space
Rounding (Li et al., 2022) and self-conditioning (Chen et al., 2023; 2026) feed the model's own token estimate back as an input, but they share the same problem, since that estimate is neither a variable of the model nor a term of its objective.
The two weaknesses are complementary, and so are their remedies. Tokens decoded in parallel need a shared state to depend on, which a continuous latent provides, and a latent being denoised needs a discrete configuration to be tied to, which the tokens provide. We therefore propose Hierarchical Continuous Diffusion Language Models (HC-DLM), a generative framework whose reverse process is a two-level chain (Fig. 1). The continuous latent trajectory {xt} is the only state that persists across steps. At every reverse step, tokens are read out from the current latent through a readout distribution pθ(kt | xt), re-noised through the discrete forward kernel, and fed back as the condition of the next latent transition pϕ(xt − 1 | xt, kt). The token state is thus a variable of the generative model with a forward kernel of its own, which is what separates the scaffold from a fed-back estimate. In the generative model, kt depends on the past only through xt, so the tokens carry no transition chain of their own and every position is read out anew at each step. We call this organization the hierarchical coupling. It determines both how the model is trained and how it samples: a single variational bound over the two-level trajectory gives the training objective (Section 3.2), and generation alternates latent denoising with token readout and re-noising (Section 3.4).
Hybrid discrete–continuous diffusion models also pair the two spaces, through per-token continuous hints (CADD) (Zheng et al., 2026), or an embedding chain denoised in parallel with the tokens (CCDD) (Zhou et al., 2026). However, separate transition chains are used as discussed in Section 5 and Appendix C.

hits.title: DuoMind: Enabling Distributed Multi-Robot Coordination with Semantic Communication
hits.authors: Hanchu Zhou, Dechen Gao, Hang Wang, Brendan Lynch, Boqi Zhao, Qiyao Ma, Raman Goyal, Junshan Zhang
hits.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) and vision-language-action models (VLAs) have recently driven rapid progress in general-purpose robots, yet most progress has focused on single-robot settings. Extending these capabilities to multi-robot systems remains challenging because robots must coordinate long-horizon behaviors while maintaining reliable, fine-grained execution. We introduce DuoMind, a distributed hierarchical framework for multi-robot coordination through semantic communication. Each robot uses a VLA-based action model for low-level execution and a VLM-based orchestrator for high-level reasoning and inter-agent coordination. At each planning step, the orchestrator at each robot reasons over the task instruction, local observations, and messages received from other robots. It then generates low-level instructions for the action model and semantic messages for peer robots. This architecture exploits the complementary strengths of pretrained models by combining the semantic reasoning capabilities of VLMs with the precise action-generation capabilities of VLAs. To address the scarcity of benchmarks for multi-robot coordination, we further develop RoboPoly, a benchmark comprising long-horizon manipulation tasks that require coordinated, closed-loop execution under distributed control. Experiments on RoboPoly and RoboTwin demonstrate that DuoMind improves multi-robot task performance, while ablation studies confirm the contributions of hierarchical orchestration and semantic communication. More details are available on our project page.

Section: 4.3 ABLATION OF INTER-AGENT COMMUNICATION

Figure 4: Ablation studies of DuoMind. (a) Success rates when inter-agent communication is disabled. (b) Success rates with different action models.
(a) Inter-agent communication ablation.
(b) Action model ablation.
Inter-agent communication provides complementary information for decision making and helps mitigate partial observability. To evaluate its effect, we conduct an ablation, following the evaluation setting in section 4.2 except that messages from peer agents are disabled. As shown in fig. 4a, removing inter-agent communication leads to more frequent conflicts and asynchronous behaviors, resulting in degraded coordination performance. These results demonstrate that explicitly sharing peer information is important for effective multi-robot coordination under distributed observations. We further elaborate the ablation study in B.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) and vision-language-action models (VLAs) have recently driven rapid progress in general-purpose robots, yet most progress has focused on single-robot settings. This architecture exploits the complementary strengths of pretrained models by combining the semantic reasoning capabilities of VLMs with the precise action-generation capabilities of VLAs. Section: B EFFECT OF INTER-AGENT COMMUNICATION

Inter-agent communication shares complementary information for decision making and helps mitigate the partial observability inherent in distributed multi-robot settings. To further study the effect of the shared messages, we conduct an ablation using DuoMind with π0 . 5 as the action model, following the evaluation setting in section 4.2 except that messages from peer agents are disabled. Under this setting, each orchestrator receives no information from the other agent during reasoning and generates low-level instructions based only on its local observation and the task instruction.
The results are reported in fig. 7. Without inter-agent communication, we observe more frequent conflicts and asynchronous behaviors between the two robots. For example, in Cook Pot, the two robots are required to lift the pot handles in a coordinated manner. Without communication, one robot often starts lifting while the other has only begun grasping the handle, causing the coordinated manipulation to fail. In Prepare Snack, the two robots may independently select the same plate as their target and attempt to place bread simultaneously, which can lead to collisions between the robot arms above the plate.
14
Figure 7: The result of ablation study that disable the inter-agent communication in DuoMind.
These failure cases illustrate a limitation of relying solely on local observations: an individual agent may not have sufficient information to infer the peer agent's current intention or upcoming behavior. Explicit inter-agent communication provides a direct and efficient mechanism for sharing such information, thereby reducing conflicts and improving synchronized and safe multi-robot coordination.

Section: 5.1 LEARNING-BASED MULTI-AGENT COORDINATION

Classical multi-agent learning studies decentralized decision-making under partial observability and non-stationarity through centralized training, value decomposition, and learned communication (Lowe et al., 2017; Rashid et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2022; Foerster et al., 2016). These methods are effective in cooperative games and simulation, but often require task-specific joint training and encode coordination in latent representations that are hard to interpret or integrate with pretrained robot foundation models. Recent work extends coordination to physical robots through decentralized imitation learning, shared representations, and VLA policies (Dong et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025; Doshi et al., 2026). In contrast, DuoMind uses decentralized reasoning with explicit natural-language communication for interpretable exchange of task-relevant information.

Section: 6 CONCLUSION

We presented DuoMind, a distributed hierarchical framework for multi-robot coordination that combines high-level reasoning, low-level control, and semantic inter-agent communication. We further introduced RoboPoly, a benchmark for evaluating long-horizon multi-robot manipulation under distributed observations and control. Experiments on RoboPoly and RoboTwin demonstrate that hierarchical orchestration improves multi-robot task execution, while ablation studies highlight the importance of explicit information sharing for coordination under partial observability. The decoupled design also allows different reasoning and action models to be integrated without redesigning the overall framework. As stronger VLMs and VLAs continue to emerge, DuoMind can naturally incorporate these advances to further improve its coordination capabilities. Leveraging such advances toward more capable and efficient real-world multi-robot coordination is a promising direction for future work.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) and vision-language-action models (VLAs) have recently driven rapid progress in general-purpose robots, yet most progress has focused on single-robot settings. Extending these capabilities to multi-robot systems remains challenging because robots must coordinate long-horizon behaviors while maintaining reliable, fine-grained execution. We introduce DuoMind, a distributed hierarchical framework for multi-robot coordination through semantic communication. Each robot uses a VLA-based action model for low-level execution and a VLM-based orchestrator for high-level reasoning and inter-agent coordination. At each planning step, the orchestrator at each robot reasons over the task instruction, local observations, and messages received from other robots. It then generates low-level instructions for the action model and semantic messages for peer robots. This architecture exploits the complementary strengths of pretrained models by combining the semantic reasoning capabilities of VLMs with the precise action-generation capabilities of VLAs. To address the scarcity of benchmarks for multi-robot coordination, we further develop RoboPoly, a benchmark comprising long-horizon manipulation tasks that require coordinated, closed-loop execution under distributed control. Experiments on RoboPoly and RoboTwin demonstrate that DuoMind improves multi-robot task performance, while ablation studies confirm the contributions of hierarchical orchestration and semantic communication. More details are available on our project page.

At each planning step, each orchestrator reasons over the high-level instruction, its local observation, and the shared message from other robots. It then generates both a low-level instruction for the action model and a structured message for other robots. These two outputs serve complementary roles. The low-level instruction guides the action model to produce fine-grained robot actions, while the message communicates the robot's intention, subgoal, and task belief, allowing each agent to remain aware of its peers despite partial observability (Liang et al., 2025b) in the distributed setting. In this way, DuoMind provides an agentic harness around the action model: the orchestrator dynamically reasons and invokes the action model to realize long-horizon coordinated behavior at a relatively low frequency, while the action model focuses on high-frequency execution. Importantly, this decoupled design allows DuoMind to capitalize on the strong pretrained capabilities of existing VLM and VLA backbones. Rather than heavily fine-tuning models specifically for multi-robot coordination, highlevel coordination and low-level manipulation can be largely handled by off-the-shelf VLM models, requiring only limited adaptation to the multi-robot setting. To systematically evaluate the coordination capabilities, we introduce RoboPoly, which provides challenging long-horizon manipulation tasks in which multiple robots must coordinate and complete the task through closed-loop physical execution rather than high-level planning alone. We further evaluate DuoMind across diverse cooperative scenarios and systematically study the contributions of hierarchical design and inter-agent communication. 2 The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: We introduce DuoMind, a distributed hierarchical framework for end-to-end multi-agent robotic coordination. DuoMind utilizes a VLM as the orchestrator at each robot for highlevel reasoning and a VLA as the action model for low-level control, enabling inter-agent semantic communication with natural language. This design harnesses the strong reasoning and control capabilities of existing foundation models to enable effective coordination in complex multi-robot tasks. We develop RoboPoly, a benchmark for long-horizon multi-robot coordination under distributed observations and control. The benchmark emphasizes closed-loop physical execution and includes tasks that are challenging for a single agent, requiring multiple agents to coordinate and schedule their behaviors throughout task execution. We conduct extensive experiments and ablation studies to evaluate DuoMind across challenging cooperative manipulation tasks on both RoboPoly and RoboTwin. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed hierarchical design in multi-robot coordination and further quantify the contributions of integrating orchestrator and inter-agent communication.

Section: 2.3 INTER-AGENT INFORMATION SHARING

Distributed multi-agent systems face the challenges of partial observability and non-stationarity: each agent has only partial knowledge of the global task state, while the environment continues to evolve as other agents act. Insufficient awareness of such information can lead to conflicting actions or ineffective collaboration. To address these challenges, DuoMind enables agents to share and integrate structured natural-language messages during high-level reasoning. These messages convey key information about other agents' decisions and task-relevant changes in the environment, providing additional context for more precise high-level reasoning. To support effective decisionmaking, we structure each shared message using four fields:
4
Intention. It is identical to the low-level instruction sent to the action model and describes the next subtask that the ego agent intends to execute. Sharing this intention makes other agents aware of the ego agent's next action, helping them avoid behaviors that may interfere with its execution.
Subgoals. This field specifies the expected task state after the ego agent completes its current subtask. It explicitly communicates the future state that the ego agent aims to achieve, allowing other agents to act proactively to facilitate task completion or avoid undesirable outcomes.
Belief of task. This part describes task-relevant information observed or inferred by the ego agent, such as the location of a key object or whether a particular subtask has been completed. For example, in a kitchen task, a robot operating near the cabinets may inform another robot preparing to cook that "the pot is in the third cabinet." Sharing such information reduces the impact of partial observability by propagating locally available knowledge across agents.
Uncertainty of belief. This optional field communicates the uncertainty associated with the ego agent's task belief. It is particularly useful in complex tasks, where information inferred through reasoning may not always be reliable. This uncertainty provides an additional confidence signal that allows the orchestrator to appropriately weigh different beliefs during high-level reasoning, especially when agents hold inconsistent beliefs or when the available information is ambiguous.
Through this structured information sharing, DuoMind provides each agent with compact contextual information about the intentions, subgoals, beliefs, and associated uncertainty of other agents. This additional context enables the orchestrator to generate more precise low-level instructions, thereby improving the safety and efficiency of multi-robot coordination.

Section: 5.2 ROBOT LEARNING AND MULTI-ROBOT PLANNING

Generalist robot policies leverage large-scale robot data and pretrained vision/language representations to map observations or language instructions to actions (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2026; Team et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026). Hierarchical approaches further separate high-level semantic reasoning from low-level continuous control (Shi et al., 2025; Intelligence et al., 2025b; Song et al., 2025a; Team et al., 2025), but mainly focus on single-robot execution. LLM- and VLM-based multi-robot systems explore task decomposition, allocation, communication, feedback, and replanning (Kannan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024b; Mandi et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2024; He et al., 2026), while typically relying on predefined skills, symbolic actions, waypoints, or motion planners. DuoMind instead combines distributed high-level reasoning and communication with VLA-based physical execution.

Section: 5.1 LEARNING-BASED MULTI-AGENT COORDINATION

Classical multi-agent learning studies decentralized decision-making under partial observability and non-stationarity through centralized training, value decomposition, and learned communication (Lowe et al., 2017; Rashid et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2022; Foerster et al., 2016). These methods are effective in cooperative games and simulation, but often require task-specific joint training and encode coordination in latent representations that are hard to interpret or integrate with pretrained robot foundation models. Recent work extends coordination to physical robots through decentralized imitation learning, shared representations, and VLA policies (Dong et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025; Doshi et al., 2026). In contrast, DuoMind uses decentralized reasoning with explicit natural-language communication for interpretable exchange of task-relevant information.

Section: 3.3 DATASETS

We construct the datasets using the motion-planning-based trajectory generation pipeline provided by ManiSkill3. For each task, we first decompose the full manipulation procedure into a sequence of key states, such as grasping, releasing, or moving toward a target location. Given these key states, the generation script invokes the motion planner to construct smooth robot trajectories between consecutive states. The spatial and temporal constraints for each trajectories are carefully designed with the planner to generate the desired multi-robot coordination demonstrations.
In addition to robot trajectories, we associate each manipulation stage with a low-level instruction for each robot describing the current behavior. It then replays the trajectory in simulator to render the RGB camera observations. The resulting dataset therefore contains visual observations, states, robot actions, high-level, and low-level language instructions for both robots. Section: 6 CONCLUSION

We presented DuoMind, a distributed hierarchical framework for multi-robot coordination that combines high-level reasoning, low-level control, and semantic inter-agent communication. We further introduced RoboPoly, a benchmark for evaluating long-horizon multi-robot manipulation under distributed observations and control. Experiments on RoboPoly and RoboTwin demonstrate that hierarchical orchestration improves multi-robot task execution, while ablation studies highlight the importance of explicit information sharing for coordination under partial observability. The decoupled design also allows different reasoning and action models to be integrated without redesigning the overall framework. As stronger VLMs and VLAs continue to emerge, DuoMind can naturally incorporate these advances to further improve its coordination capabilities. Leveraging such advances toward more capable and efficient real-world multi-robot coordination is a promising direction for future work.

Section: 5.3 ROBOT LEARNING AND MULTI-AGENT BENCHMARKS

Established robot-learning benchmarks provide diverse manipulation tasks, demonstrations, language instructions, and long-horizon evaluation, but largely focus on single robots or centrally controlled embodiments (Yu et al., 2020; James et al., 2020; Gu et al., 2023; Mees et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023). Recent multi-agent benchmarks study collaborative planning, heterogeneous capabilities, and manipulation (Mandi et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b; Chang et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025). However, they often emphasize either abstract high-level planning or low-level manipulation. RoboPoly instead evaluates long-horizon coordination and closed-loop execution under distributed observation and control.

All tasks share a common workspace configuration with two robot arms positioned on opposite sides of a table. The workspace and object placement are designed such that a single robot cannot always complete the task independently or efficiently, making cooperation necessary. RoboPoly contains the following seven tasks: Food Serve, Prepare Snack, Clean Table, Cook Pot, Put Object Cabinet, Hang Bag, Exchange Bread. We further detail the task description in A.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) and vision-language-action models (VLAs) have recently driven rapid progress in general-purpose robots, yet most progress has focused on single-robot settings. More details are available on our project page.

Section: 2.1 MULTI-AGENT COORDINATION VIA EMBODIED REASONING

Existing studies on hierarchical robotic architectures have shown that action models are effective at low-level control and instruction following when provided with specific commands (Team et al., 2025). To extend this capability toward more general and long-horizon tasks, a promising approach is to introduce a reasoning model as an orchestrator, leveraging its strong visual understanding, semantic grounding, and planning capabilities to generate appropriate instructions for the action model. In distributed multi-agent settings, where task coordination are substantially more complex, we extend this hierarchical paradigm to distributed multi-robot coordination in DuoMind.
3
Specifically, DuoMind decomposes multi-agent coordination into two complementary levels: highlevel multi-agent reasoning and low-level execution. Each robot employs a VLM as an orchestrator that reasons over the task-level instruction, its local visual observation, and message shared by other agents. The orchestrator determines the robot's current subtask and translates it into a single-agent, short-horizon instruction for low-level control. The VLA, serving as the action model, then follows the low-level instruction using local observations to generate fine-grained robot actions. This division of responsibility allows each module to focus on the capability for which it is best suited: the orchestrator handles high-level understanding and inter-agent coordination in multi-agent setting, while the action model performs reliable low-level control.
Importantly, this decomposition avoids requiring the action model to directly interpret complex multi-agent state that includes the joint behavior of multiple robots and environment, which can be extremely challenging since action models are primarily trained with single-agent demonstrations. It therefore decouples multi-agent reasoning from low-level control, reducing the need for the action model itself to possess strong reasoning capabilities for multi-agent coordination. Moreover, DuoMind does not require the orchestrator, the action model, or the interface between them to be extensively redesigned for multi-agent settings. These foundation models developed for single-agent systems can be reused largely off the shelf, with only lightweight adaptation when necessary. This greatly extends the possibility of deploying DuoMind to diverse multi-robot tasks and offers strong compatibility to future upgrades on components.
The design of DuoMind naturally supports coordination among multiple robots. However, the complexity of task design, data collection, and evaluation increases substantially as the number of agents grows. Considering the high computational cost when the number of robots scales up, we focus on two-agent settings in this work and leave coordination at larger team scales for future study.

Section: A TASK SETTINGS OF ROBOPOLY

RoboPoly contains the following seven tasks:
Food Serve. Two pieces of bread and a serving tray are placed across the workspace such that one robot cannot reach both the bread and the tray. The robots must transfer the bread between each other when necessary and place both pieces onto the tray.
Prepare Snack. Two plates are placed near the center of the table, while four pieces of bread are distributed across the two sides of the workspace. The robots must place two pieces on each plate. Both robots can operate simultaneously and must coordinate their motions to efficiently complete the task while avoiding collisions.
Clean Table. Two cubes and a container are placed on the table such that neither robot can independently reach all cubes and container. Completing the task requires a cube to be passed between the robots when the container lies outside the workspace of a robot.
Cook Pot. A carrot, a pot with a lid, and an oven are placed around the center of the workspace. The robots must first remove the lid, place the carrot into the pot, and replace the lid. They should then jointly grasp the two handles of the pot and transport it to the oven.
13
Put Object Cabinet. A cube and a cabinet are placed in the workspace. The robots must open the bottom drawer of the cabinet, place the cube inside, and close the drawer. The task requires coordination between two robot arms for higher efficiency.
Hang Bag. A bag and a hook are placed on opposite sides of the workspace such that neither robot can reach both. One robot must first pass the bag to the other robot, which then hangs the bag onto the hook.
Exchange Bread. A piece of bread and a target box are placed beside each robot arm. Each robot must place its own bread into the box on the opposite side of the table. Since the target box lies outside its reachable workspace, the robot must first hand the bread over to the other robot, which then places it into the corresponding box.

DuoMind: Enabling Distributed Multi-Robot Coordination with Semantic Communication

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) and vision-language-action models (VLAs) have recently driven rapid progress in general-purpose robots, yet most progress has focused on single-robot settings. Extending these capabilities to multi-robot systems remains challenging because robots must coordinate long-horizon behaviors while maintaining reliable, fine-grained execution. We introduce DuoMind, a distributed hierarchical framework for multi-robot coordination through semantic communication. Each robot uses a VLA-based action model for low-level execution and a VLM-based orchestrator for high-level reasoning and inter-agent coordination. At each planning step, the orchestrator at each robot reasons over the task instruction, local observations, and messages received from other robots. It then generates low-level instructions for the action model and semantic messages for peer robots. This architecture exploits the complementary strengths of pretrained models by combining the semantic reasoning capabilities of VLMs with the precise action-generation capabilities of VLAs. To address the scarcity of benchmarks for multi-robot coordination, we further develop RoboPoly, a benchmark comprising long-horizon manipulation tasks that require coordinated, closed-loop execution under distributed control. Experiments on RoboPoly and RoboTwin demonstrate that DuoMind improves multi-robot task performance, while ablation studies confirm the contributions of hierarchical orchestration and semantic communication. More details are available on our project page.

At each planning step, each orchestrator reasons over the high-level instruction, its local observation, and the shared message from other robots. It then generates both a low-level instruction for the action model and a structured message for other robots. These two outputs serve complementary roles. The low-level instruction guides the action model to produce fine-grained robot actions, while the message communicates the robot's intention, subgoal, and task belief, allowing each agent to remain aware of its peers despite partial observability (Liang et al., 2025b) in the distributed setting. In this way, DuoMind provides an agentic harness around the action model: the orchestrator dynamically reasons and invokes the action model to realize long-horizon coordinated behavior at a relatively low frequency, while the action model focuses on high-frequency execution. Importantly, this decoupled design allows DuoMind to capitalize on the strong pretrained capabilities of existing VLM and VLA backbones. Rather than heavily fine-tuning models specifically for multi-robot coordination, highlevel coordination and low-level manipulation can be largely handled by off-the-shelf VLM models, requiring only limited adaptation to the multi-robot setting. To systematically evaluate the coordination capabilities, we introduce RoboPoly, which provides challenging long-horizon manipulation tasks in which multiple robots must coordinate and complete the task through closed-loop physical execution rather than high-level planning alone. We further evaluate DuoMind across diverse cooperative scenarios and systematically study the contributions of hierarchical design and inter-agent communication. 2 The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: We introduce DuoMind, a distributed hierarchical framework for end-to-end multi-agent robotic coordination. DuoMind utilizes a VLM as the orchestrator at each robot for highlevel reasoning and a VLA as the action model for low-level control, enabling inter-agent semantic communication with natural language. This design harnesses the strong reasoning and control capabilities of existing foundation models to enable effective coordination in complex multi-robot tasks. We develop RoboPoly, a benchmark for long-horizon multi-robot coordination under distributed observations and control. The benchmark emphasizes closed-loop physical execution and includes tasks that are challenging for a single agent, requiring multiple agents to coordinate and schedule their behaviors throughout task execution. We conduct extensive experiments and ablation studies to evaluate DuoMind across challenging cooperative manipulation tasks on both RoboPoly and RoboTwin. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed hierarchical design in multi-robot coordination and further quantify the contributions of integrating orchestrator and inter-agent communication.

hits.title: SHARPO: Segment-Level Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
hits.authors: Xinchen Du, Zhengze Zhou, Wenhui Zhu, Han Yu, Sen Na, Rohit Jain, Alborz Geramifard
hits.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) trains a large language model (LLM) to act over long, multi-step interactions. However, a single localized error can cause task failure, while trajectory-level rewards provide limited guidance for assigning credit to individual decisions. To address this limitation, we introduce Segment-level Hindsight Advantage Reweighting for Policy Optimization (SHARPO), a credit-assignment mechanism that refines Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) at the level of environment-facing segments. Inspired by the existing on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) method, SHARPO computes teacher-student log-probability gaps within each segment and uses the resulting signal to compute a bounded multiplier on the GRPO advantage. This multiplier is shared by all tokens within the segment, allowing credit to vary across different segments. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, SHARPO outperforms existing baselines on the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks, including GRPO, SDAR, RLSD, and StepOPSD.

Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) trains a large language model (LLM) to act over long, multi-step interactions. However, a single localized error can cause task failure, while trajectory-level rewards provide limited guidance for assigning credit to individual decisions. To address this limitation, we introduce Segment-level Hindsight Advantage Reweighting for Policy Optimization (SHARPO), a credit-assignment mechanism that refines Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) at the level of environment-facing segments. Section: 5 Conclusion

SHARPO refines GRPO credit using successful-peer feedback on intermediate interaction segments. It aggregates teacher-student log-probability gaps within each segment and applies a shared, bounded adjustment to the outcome-derived advantage. The analysis explains how ideal success-conditioned feedback refines local credit. On ALFWorld and WebShop, the method improves final validation success over GRPO and the evaluated self-distillation baselines at both tested mixing weights. These results support using meaningful interaction segments to organize self-distillation feedback for agent training.

Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) trains a large language model (LLM) to act over long, multi-step interactions. However, a single localized error can cause task failure, while trajectory-level rewards provide limited guidance for assigning credit to individual decisions. To address this limitation, we introduce Segment-level Hindsight Advantage Reweighting for Policy Optimization (SHARPO), a credit-assignment mechanism that refines Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) at the level of environment-facing segments. Inspired by the existing on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) method, SHARPO computes teacher-student log-probability gaps within each segment and uses the resulting signal to compute a bounded multiplier on the GRPO advantage. This multiplier is shared by all tokens within the segment, allowing credit to vary across different segments. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, SHARPO outperforms existing baselines on the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks, including GRPO, SDAR, RLSD, and StepOPSD.

Concretely, we instantiate the teacher as a copy of the agent's policy and compute teacher-student log-probability differences. These differences indicate how strongly the teacher supports the sampled behavior relative to the student. We then use this signal to adjust the magnitude of GRPO's outcome-derived advantages. To sum up, our method SHARPO combines fine-grained guidance from self-distillation with task-level supervision from environmental rewards. In an interactive task, a trajectory contains semantically meaningful spans, such as agent reasoning, tool calls, and actions. We refer to these spans as interaction segments and use those as the units for refining credit assignment. For each selected segment, SHARPO assigns a weight based on the teacher-student log-probability difference for that segment. This weight scales the GRPO advantage uniformly within its segment, refining how the trajectory-level reward outcome is credited to intermediate substeps. By incorporating the teacher's assessment of each substep, SHARPO provides local guidance on the strength of reinforcement or penalization, alleviating the creditassignment problem caused by sparse terminal rewards. This segment-level formulation distinguishes SHARPO from related approaches in how teacher feedback is organized and used for credit assignment. Unlike RLSD [Yang et al., 2026], which reweights token-level advantages using self-divergence, or SDAR [Lu et al., 2026], which applies soft token-level gating to an auxiliary distillation loss over the full response, SHARPO aggregates teacher feedback within selected interaction segments and assigns a shared advantage weight to each segment. Compared to StepOPSD [Zhang et al., 2026], which retains token-specific weights within selected action-centered spans, SHARPO aggregates the feedback within each segment before determining its weight. Favorable and unfavorable evidence across a substep is therefore considered jointly, allowing the credit adjustment to reflect the teacher's overall support for the complete decision. We evaluate SHARPO on ALFWorld and WebShop using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. As shown in Figure 1, SHARPO achieves higher final validation success rates than baselines on both benchmarks at both parameter configurations. To summarize, our main contributions are threefold: We propose SHARPO, a segment-level credit-assignment method that uses successful peer rollouts to guide the weighting of intermediate decisions in GRPO. By aggregating selfdistillation feedback over meaningful interaction segments, it supplements sparse outcome supervision without requiring an external teacher or additional environment rollouts. 2 We provide a theoretical explanation of why this self-distillation feedback is useful in our method and how it supports finer-grained credit assignment. We demonstrate that SHARPO outperforms GRPO, RLSD, SDAR, and StepOPSD on both ALFWorld and WebShop. Analyses of subtask success rates and product-matching quality further characterize these gains.\n\nSection: 2 Method

We first review GRPO and OPSD in Section 2.1 and then present SHARPO in Section 2.2. Section 2.3 provides a theoretical analysis of our segment-level credit assignment.

To address this limitation, we introduce Segment-level Hindsight Advantage Reweighting for Policy Optimization (SHARPO), a credit-assignment mechanism that refines Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) at the level of environment-facing segments. Inspired by the existing on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) method, SHARPO computes teacher-student log-probability gaps within each segment and uses the resulting signal to compute a bounded multiplier on the GRPO advantage. This multiplier is shared by all tokens within the segment, allowing credit to vary across different segments. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, SHARPO outperforms existing baselines on the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks, including GRPO, SDAR, RLSD, and StepOPSD.

Section: 3.2 Main results

Table 1 reports the overall comparison. SHARPO achieves the highest mean final validation success rate on both benchmarks at both tested mixing weights. Relative to GRPO, the gains are 13.80-14.32 percentage points on ALFWorld and 8.85-9.11 points on WebShop. Compared with StepOPSD at the corresponding reported λ values, SHARPO gains 6.77 points on ALFWorld at both settings and 5.99-7.55 points on WebShop. These results support the effectiveness of using segment-level self-distillation feedback to refine GRPO credit assignment.
The improvements persist across both tested mixing weights. Although λ = 0.2 and λ = 0.05 differ by a factor of four, their mean success rates differ by only 0.52 percentage points on ALFWorld and 0.26 points on WebShop. Across the three independent runs, SHARPO has lower variability than GRPO on ALFWorld, with standard deviations of 2.82 and 1.19 points compared with 7.83. On WebShop, its standard deviations of 1.19 and 1.35 points are comparable to GRPO's 1.19. The higher mean success rates therefore accompany lower run-to-run variability on ALFWorld and similar variability on WebShop.

SHARPO: Segment-Level Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning

Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) trains a large language model (LLM) to act over long, multi-step interactions. However, a single localized error can cause task failure, while trajectory-level rewards provide limited guidance for assigning credit to individual decisions. To address this limitation, we introduce Segment-level Hindsight Advantage Reweighting for Policy Optimization (SHARPO), a credit-assignment mechanism that refines Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) at the level of environment-facing segments. Inspired by the existing on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) method, SHARPO computes teacher-student log-probability gaps within each segment and uses the resulting signal to compute a bounded multiplier on the GRPO advantage. This multiplier is shared by all tokens within the segment, allowing credit to vary across different segments. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, SHARPO outperforms existing baselines on the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks, including GRPO, SDAR, RLSD, and StepOPSD.

Section: 1 Introduction Post-training plays a key role in adapting large language models (LLMs) to specific tasks and improving their performance in interactive environments [Ouyang et al., 2022, Jin et al., 2025]. Reinforcement learning (RL) supports this adaptation by optimizing agent behavior using feedback from task outcomes. When these outcomes can be automatically verified, their correctness provides a direct reward signal for training, as demonstrated in mathematical reasoning and search-based question answering [Guo et al., 2025a, Jin et al., 2025]. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) offers an efficient approach to learning from such rewards without training a separate value network [Shao et al., 2024]. For each task, GRPO samples a group of rollouts and normalizes their rewards within the group to estimate advantages. Under outcome supervision, each rollout receives a single advantage that is shared by all of its generated tokens. In multi-turn interactions, however, an agent must make a sequence of decisions before receiving feedback on the final outcome. In this case, the rewards are sparse and are available only at the end of an episode, hence they provide little direct information about the contribution of each intermediate step to that outcome. For example, a shopping agent may find a suitable product but select an incorrect option before completing the purchase. If the resulting trajectory receives a negative advantage, both the useful search and the mistaken selection inherit the same negative coefficient. The shared advantage therefore does not distinguish actions that helped accomplish the task from those that led to failure. This motivates us to design a credit-assignment mechanism in RL that uses finer-grained signals to refine the credit assigned to individual decisions within a trajectory. One source of such fine-grained signals is on-policy distillation (OPD), where a student learns from a teacher's token-level predictions on responses generated by the student itself [Agarwal et al., 2024]. ∗Work done during an internship at LinkedIn Corporation. SHARPO improves on GRPO at both mixing weights on both benchmarks, reaching 84.90% on ALFWorld (+14.32 points) and 75.26% on WebShop (+9.11 points). Bars are means over three independent runs at training step 200; the vertical axis starts at 50%. Table 1 reports all baselines with standard deviations. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) removes this dependence by using the same LLM as both teacher and student under different conditioning contexts [Zhao et al., 2026]. The teacher receives privileged information, such as a reference solution, and guides the student on its own rollouts. Therefore, OPSD provides dense training feedback without requiring an external teacher model. Inspired by OPSD, our SHARPO reuses a successful rollout from the same GRPO group to show the teacher how the task can be completed. The teacher uses this additional information to evaluate the student's behavior and provide feedback for credit assignment within the trajectory. Concretely, we instantiate the teacher as a copy of the agent's policy and compute teacher-student log-probability differences. These differences indicate how strongly the teacher supports the sampled behavior relative to the student. We then use this signal to adjust the magnitude of GRPO's outcome-derived advantages. To sum up, our method SHARPO combines fine-grained guidance from self-distillation with task-level supervision from environmental rewards. SHARPO: Segment-Level Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning

Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) trains a large language model (LLM) to act over long, multi-step interactions. However, a single localized error can cause task failure, while trajectory-level rewards provide limited guidance for assigning credit to individual decisions. To address this limitation, we introduce Segment-level Hindsight Advantage Reweighting for Policy Optimization (SHARPO), a credit-assignment mechanism that refines Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) at the level of environment-facing segments. Inspired by the existing on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) method, SHARPO computes teacher-student log-probability gaps within each segment and uses the resulting signal to compute a bounded multiplier on the GRPO advantage. This multiplier is shared by all tokens within the segment, allowing credit to vary across different segments. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, SHARPO outperforms existing baselines on the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks, including GRPO, SDAR, RLSD, and StepOPSD.

Section: 4 RelatedWork

Outcome-supervised RL has been applied to reasoning models [Shao et al., 2024, Guo et al., 2025a] and multi-turn language agents [Jin et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2025]. Actor-critic implementations of PPO [Schulman et al., 2017] commonly pair a learned value function with generalized advantage estimation (GAE) [Schulman et al., 2016], which combines temporal-difference residuals across time in a construction related to eligibility traces. ArCHer treats utterances as high-level actions and uses off-policy critic learning to obtain utterance-level advantages for token-level policy updates [Zhou et al., 2024]. Other approaches use recurring environment states [Feng et al., 2025], Monte Carlo resampling [Kazemnejad et al., 2025, Guo et al., 2025b], or process reward models [Lightman et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2024]. TRIAGE assigns credit to role-typed environment-facing segments [Xu et al., 2026], while POAD studies action-level optimization [Wen et al., 2024]. In comparison, our method SHARPO retains GRPO's critic-free trajectory advantage and obtains local feedback by scoring sampled segments under student and successful-peer-conditioned teacher policies. The resulting log-probability gaps determine bounded weights shared within each selected segment. This provides segment-specific credit without fitting a critic to expected task returns or using temporaldifference backups, external judges, or additional environment rollouts.
8
This use of successful-peer context is related to context distillation, which transfers behavior induced by privileged context [Snell et al., 2022]. On-policy distillation evaluates the student's own samples [Agarwal et al., 2024]. OPSD uses the same model under different conditioning contexts [Zhao et al., 2026]. RLSD applies self-distillation gaps to token-level advantage magnitudes [Yang et al., 2026]; SDAR gates an auxiliary distillation objective [Lu et al., 2026]; and StepOPSD uses successful-peer hindsight for token-specific weighting within action-centered spans [Zhang et al., 2026]. SHARPO instead aggregates feedback over each selected segment before weighting its GRPO advantage. Concurrent AgentOPSD aggregates feedback over full turns using a retrieved skill and a recursive belief update [Wang et al., 2026]; our method uses independently scored environment-facing segments and successful peers from the current group.

SHARPO: Segment-Level Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning

Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) trains a large language model (LLM) to act over long, multi-step interactions. However, a single localized error can cause task failure, while trajectory-level rewards provide limited guidance for assigning credit to individual decisions. To address this limitation, we introduce Segment-level Hindsight Advantage Reweighting for Policy Optimization (SHARPO), a credit-assignment mechanism that refines Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) at the level of environment-facing segments. Inspired by the existing on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) method, SHARPO computes teacher-student log-probability gaps within each segment and uses the resulting signal to compute a bounded multiplier on the GRPO advantage. This multiplier is shared by all tokens within the segment, allowing credit to vary across different segments. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, SHARPO outperforms existing baselines on the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks, including GRPO, SDAR, RLSD, and StepOPSD.

task can be completed. The teacher uses this additional information to evaluate the student's behavior and provide feedback for credit assignment within the trajectory. Concretely, we instantiate the teacher as a copy of the agent's policy and compute teacher-student log-probability differences. These differences indicate how strongly the teacher supports the sampled behavior relative to the student. We then use this signal to adjust the magnitude of GRPO's outcome-derived advantages. To sum up, our method SHARPO combines fine-grained guidance from self-distillation with task-level supervision from environmental rewards. In an interactive task, a trajectory contains semantically meaningful spans, such as agent reasoning, tool calls, and actions. We refer to these spans as interaction segments and use those as the units for refining credit assignment. For each selected segment, SHARPO assigns a weight based on the teacher-student log-probability difference for that segment. This weight scales the GRPO advantage uniformly within its segment, refining how the trajectory-level reward outcome is credited to intermediate substeps. By incorporating the teacher's assessment of each substep, SHARPO provides local guidance on the strength of reinforcement or penalization, alleviating the creditassignment problem caused by sparse terminal rewards. This segment-level formulation distinguishes SHARPO from related approaches in how teacher feedback is organized and used for credit assignment. Unlike RLSD [Yang et al., 2026], which reweights token-level advantages using self-divergence, or SDAR [Lu et al., 2026], which applies soft token-level gating to an auxiliary distillation loss over the full response, SHARPO aggregates teacher feedback within selected interaction segments and assigns a shared advantage weight to each segment. Compared to StepOPSD [Zhang et al., 2026], which retains token-specific weights within selected action-centered spans, SHARPO aggregates the feedback within each segment before determining its weight. Favorable and unfavorable evidence across a substep is therefore considered jointly, allowing the credit adjustment to reflect the teacher's overall support for the complete decision. We evaluate SHARPO on ALFWorld and WebShop using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. As shown in Figure 1, SHARPO achieves higher final validation success rates than baselines on both benchmarks at both parameter configurations. To summarize, our main contributions are threefold: We propose SHARPO, a segment-level credit-assignment method that uses successful peer rollouts to guide the weighting of intermediate decisions in GRPO. By aggregating selfdistillation feedback over meaningful interaction segments, it supplements sparse outcome supervision without requiring an external teacher or additional environment rollouts. 2 We provide a theoretical explanation of why this self-distillation feedback is useful in our method and how it supports finer-grained credit assignment. We demonstrate that SHARPO outperforms GRPO, RLSD, SDAR, and StepOPSD on both ALFWorld and WebShop. Analyses of subtask success rates and product-matching quality further characterize these gains.\n\nSection: 2 Method

We first review GRPO and OPSD in Section 2.1 and then present SHARPO in Section 2.2. Section 2.3 provides a theoretical analysis of our segment-level credit assignment.

Section: 3.2 Main results

Table 1 reports the overall comparison. SHARPO achieves the highest mean final validation success rate on both benchmarks at both tested mixing weights. Relative to GRPO, the gains are 13.80-14.32 percentage points on ALFWorld and 8.85-9.11 points on WebShop. Compared with StepOPSD at the corresponding reported λ values, SHARPO gains 6.77 points on ALFWorld at both settings and 5.99-7.55 points on WebShop. These results support the effectiveness of using segment-level self-distillation feedback to refine GRPO credit assignment.
The improvements persist across both tested mixing weights. Although λ = 0.2 and λ = 0.05 differ by a factor of four, their mean success rates differ by only 0.52 percentage points on ALFWorld and 0.26 points on WebShop. Across the three independent runs, SHARPO has lower variability than GRPO on ALFWorld, with standard deviations of 2.82 and 1.19 points compared with 7.83. On WebShop, its standard deviations of 1.19 and 1.35 points are comparable to GRPO's 1.19. The higher mean success rates therefore accompany lower run-to-run variability on ALFWorld and similar variability on WebShop.

hits.title: SILSA: Sliding-Window Slice Latents for Topology-Preserving High-Resolution 3D Generation
hits.authors: Tianjiao Yu, Xinzhuo Li, Yifan Shen, Ying Shen, Kiet A. Nguyen, Adheesh Sunil Juvekar, Ismini Lourentzou
hits.abstract: High-resolution 3D generation increasingly relies on voxel latents and multi-stage pipelines that first predict active structure and then synthesize local geometry. While effective, this design fragments continuous surfaces into many local tokens, inflates generation cost, and often weakens topological consistency for thin or highly connected shapes. We introduce SILSA, a topology-aware 3D generation framework that represents shapes with compact sliding-window slice latents. Instead of generating expensive voxel tokens, SILSA uses a fixed set of overlapping slices along the three canonical axes, where each token summarizes a local depth window to preserve cross-sectional continuity and support single-stage rectified-flow generation. A Slice VAE encodes oriented surface samples into multi-axis slice latents and reconstructs them with a sparse volumetric decoder, while a Volumetric Anchor Lattice coordinates directional slice streams through a shared 3D workspace. To preserve structural correctness, we introduce slice-level topology supervision that matches persistence diagrams and aligns Betti transitions across neighboring slices. Experiments show that SILSA improves structural fidelity while substantially reducing generation cost. SILSA improves PSNR by $8.7\%$, coverage by $5.96$ absolute points, and Betti error by $9.2\%$ over the strongest baseline, while using $70.0\%$ fewer tokens than the next-most compact baseline and over $98\%$ fewer tokens than sparse or hierarchical tokenizers, effectively reducing training memory by $40.4\%$ and inference time by $58.5\%$. Qualitative results further show improved preservation of thin structures, repeated components, and long-range connectivity.
