SILSA: Sliding-Window Slice Latents for Topology-Preserving High-Resolution 3D Generation

Abstract: High-resolution 3D generation increasingly relies on voxel latents and multi-stage pipelines that first predict active structure and then synthesize local geometry. While effective, this design fragments continuous surfaces into many local tokens, inflates generation cost, and often weakens topological consistency for thin or highly connected shapes. We introduce SILSA, a topology-aware 3D generation framework that represents shapes with compact sliding-window slice latents. Instead of generating expensive voxel tokens, SILSA uses a fixed set of overlapping slices along the three canonical axes, where each token summarizes a local depth window to preserve cross-sectional continuity and support single-stage rectified-flow generation. A Slice VAE encodes oriented surface samples into multi-axis slice latents and reconstructs them with a sparse volumetric decoder, while a Volumetric Anchor Lattice coordinates directional slice streams through a shared 3D workspace. To preserve structural correctness, we introduce slice-level topology supervision that matches persistence diagrams and aligns Betti transitions across neighboring slices. Experiments show that SILSA improves structural fidelity while substantially reducing generation cost. SILSA improves PSNR by $8.7\%$, coverage by $5.96$ absolute points, and Betti error by $9.2\%$ over the strongest baseline, while using $70.0\%$ fewer tokens than the next-most compact baseline and over $98\%$ fewer tokens than sparse or hierarchical tokenizers, effectively reducing training memory by $40.4\%$ and inference time by $58.5\%$. Qualitative results further show improved preservation of thin structures, repeated components, and long-range connectivity.

Section: A Related Work

3D Generation. Early 3D generation methods commonly adapt pretrained 2D diffusion models to optimize each target asset through differentiable rendering or score distillation [52 , 38 , 70 , 7 , 43]. These methods reduce the need for large-scale 3D supervision, but they are often heavy in optimization and may inherit multi-view inconsistency from image priors. For image-conditioned generation, multi-view diffusion and reconstruction systems improve single-view consistency by predicting viewconsistent observations before 3D reconstruction [44 , 45 , 60 , 88 , 43 , 71 , 42 , 72 , 12 , 68 , 78 , 40 , 83 , 23]. To improve scalability, later methods learn generative priors directly over compact 3D representations, including implicit fields, SDF latents, point or set latents, triplanes, and aligned image-text-shape latent spaces [79 , 37 , 31 , 90 , 69 , 13 , 33 , 85 , 6 , 27 , 82]. Recent systems further scale native 3D diffusion or rectified-flow transformers over learned latent tokens, Gaussian features, and sparse structured grids for high-quality conditioned asset generation [87 , 66 , 76 , 89 , 25]. In contrast, SILSA represents geometry as canonical slices along multiple axes, producing compact and spatially grounded latent tokens without explicitly predicting active voxels.
Latent Representations for 3D Shapes. Designing compact but expressive latent representations is central to scalable 3D modeling [51 , 47 , 5 , 85 , 76 , 8 , 80]. Dense voxel grids provide explicit spatial structure but scale cubically with resolution [74 , 14], motivating factorized representations such as triplanes and higher-dimensional plane decompositions, which encode 3D structure through axis-aligned feature planes rather than full volumetric grids [5 , 20 , 24]. Another line of work represents shapes with continuous implicit fields, including SDFs and occupancy functions, or compresses them into compact generative latents, volumetric codes, and unordered token sets [51 , 47 , 11 , 13 , 33 , 85 , 90 , 87 , 8]. These representations improve generative efficiency but often weaken explicit spatial correspondence between tokens and local geometry. A complementary direction preserves spatial locality through sparse or hierarchical voxels, reducing memory by modeling only occupied, adjacent, or progressively refined regions [56 , 67 , 55 , 76 , 25 , 75]. OReX [57] shows that sparse planar cross-sections contain rich geometric information for neural-field reconstruction. Our representation differs by using axis-aligned slices not as external observations, but as a learned generative latent: a compact 3N-token layout that combines the spatial grounding of plane-based features with the bounded token count of set-based representations.
Topology-Aware Learning. Topology-aware learning uses algebraic-topology tools, especially persistent homology [19 , 92 , 15 , 22], to supervise structural properties that are poorly captured by pointwise or pixel-wise losses. In segmentation, persistent-homology and Betti-based objectives encourage predictions to match target connectivity and hole structure, while skeleton-based losses such as clDice provide efficient topology-preserving surrogates for curvilinear objects [30 , 16 , 62 , 4 , 65 , 29]. Beyond output supervision, topology has also been used to regularize learned manifolds, as in Topological Autoencoders [49]. Recent work extends these ideas to 3D, including efficient Betti matching for volumetric segmentation, topology-constrained neural implicit reconstruction, and topology-aware reconstruction losses [64 , 32 , 86 , 59 , 28]. However, applying full volumetric persistent-homology supervision inside high-resolution generative training remains expensive, especially when topology must be evaluated repeatedly across decoded samples. SILSA makes topology supervision tractable by aligning the representation with axis-aligned cross-sections: persistent diagrams are matched within individual slices, while Betti transitions are matched across neighboring slices to preserve where topological events occur along each canonical axis.

generation. To make this representation effective for generation, SILSA combines compact slice latents with crossaxis coordination and topology-aware training. First, a SliceVAE encodes oriented surface samples into overlapping slice latents and reconstructs them through a sparse volumetric decoder, preserving local surface geometry. A Volumetric Anchor Lattice then coordinates the three directional slice streams inside the rectified-flow transformer: each slice token reads from and writes to the anchor plane associated with its axis and depth position, allowing x-, y-, and z-aligned evidence to accumulate in a shared 3D workspace and form a single coherent shape. Finally, slice-level topology losses supervise the decoded cross-sections by matching persistent-homology structure and aligning Betti transitions across adjacent slices [19 , 92 , 30 , 16 , 65 , 64]. Experiments show that SILSA improves high-resolution image-to-3D generation while substantially reducing generation cost. Across both settings, SILSA preserves fine structures that are commonly degraded by compact 3D latents, including thin supports, handles, holes, spokes, railings, and repeated parts. Empirically, SILSA improves both structural fidelity and efficiency. On image-conditioned 3D generation, it achieves the best FD, PSNR, coverage, and MMD, with an 8 . 7% relative gain in PSNR and a 5 . 96-point absolute gain in coverage over the strongest baselines, while matching the best KD and LPIPS. The SliceVAE further reduces Betti error by 9 . 2% relative to the strongest reconstruction baseline, indicating better preservation of connected components and holes. At the same time, SILSA uses only 384 fixed slice tokens, 70 . 0% fewer than the next-most compact baseline, reducing training memory by 40 . 4% and inference time by 58 . 5%. Qualitative results further show that crossaxis coordination through the Volumetric Anchor Lattice reduces inconsistent slice predictions and produces more coherent 3D assets. In summary, the contributions of our work are: 2 We introduce SILSA, a topology-aware image-to-3D generation framework that encodes shapes into a compact set of spatially grounded sliding-window slice latents across three canonical axes. We design a topology-aware SliceVAE that combines overlapping slice aggregation, sparse volumetric decoding, persistent-homology matching, and Betti-transition supervision to preserve surface geometry, connected components, and hole structures. We develop a single-stage rectified-flow generator with a Volumetric Anchor Lattice, enabling cross-axis coordination through shared spatial memory and efficient image-conditioned 3D generation from only 384 slice tokens.

Section: 2 Related Work

High-resolution 3D generation has evolved from lifting 2D diffusion priors through score distillation and differentiable rendering [52 , 38 , 70 , 7] to image-conditioned multi-view reconstruction pipelines [44 , 45 , 60 , 42 , 61] and native 3D generators over learned latent spaces [13 , 33 , 90 , 87 , 76 , 75 , 25 , 80]. Existing 3D representations trade off efficiency and structure: dense voxels provide spatial grounding but scale cubically [74 , 13], triplanes and set latents improve compactness but weaken local geometric correspondence [5 , 20 , 85], and sparse or hierarchical voxel tokenizers preserve locality but require data-dependent token counts and often multi-stage generation [55 , 76 , 25]. Crosssectional representations provide a spatially grounded alternative, as planar slices expose components, holes, and connectivity changes that compact global latents can blur, while OReX [57] demonstrates that such slices provide useful geometric cues for reconstruction. SILSA differs by using multi-axis cross-sections as a learned generative latent with fixed sliding-window slice tokens. Moreover, our topology supervision builds on persistent homology and Betti-based losses for preserving connectivity and holes [19 , 92 , 30 , 16 , 64], but avoids expensive full-volume topology matching by supervising persistence within slices and Betti transitions across neighboring slices. Additional discussion of 3D generation, latent 3D representations, and topology-aware learning is provided in Appendix A.

Section: 3 Method

State-of-the-art 3D generative models encode shapes into structured latent tokens and generate them with transformer-based diffusion or rectified-flow models [76 , 25]. The token count, however, scales with surface area, making generation expensive and requiring multi-stage pipelines that first predict which voxels are active before generating their structured latents. Beyond efficiency, voxellevel tokenization also fragments continuous surfaces into many local elements, making topological coherence challenging to model.
We propose SILSA to address these limitations by generating compact, spatially grounded slice latents (Figure 2). First, we introduce a SliceVAE that maps 3D shapes to compact multi-axis slice latents and decodes them into a high-resolution mesh (§3.1). The encoder aggregates surface points with overlapping sliding windows along the three canonical axes, yielding a compact set of tokens that preserves local cross-sectional structure. The decoder populates a volumetric feature grid from these tokens and reconstructs geometry through sparse volumetric upsampling. To preserve structural correctness, we further introduce a Slice-Wise Topology-Preserving Loss that supervises decoded cross-sections (§3.2). Second, we train a rectified flow transformer to generate slice latents from an input image (§3.3). Since the slice layout is fixed, generation does not require a separate active-voxel prediction stage. Instead, we introduce a Volumetric Anchor Lattice (VAL), a shared spatial memory that enables slice tokens from different axes to read and write axis-aligned anchor planes during denoising.

Section: D Additional Results

Open Surface Evaluation. We further evaluate SliceVAE on the open-surface dataset DeepFashion3D [91]. As shown in Table 5, SILSA achieves the best reconstruction quality across geometric metrics, reducing CD from 0.05 to 0.04 over SparseFlex while matching its perfect F-Score@0.01 and improving F-Score@0.005 from 93.07 to 93.21. Topology-aware metrics saturate on this dataset because garments are topologically simple, so all methods that recover the rough surface achieve near-zero Betti-Err. The geometric improvements demonstrate that the slice-latent representation generalizes to open-surface shapes.
Image-to-3D in the Wild. Figure 6 shows image-conditioned generations on diverse in-the-wild examples. SILSA recovers plausible 3D structure from a single view and maintains consistency across rendered viewpoints. The results are strongest on objects whose geometry is difficult for compact global latents, including chairs with legs and armrests, drones with thin propeller supports, motorcycles with wheels and handles, and flowers with layered petals. These examples show that the proposed cross-axis slice representation provides enough local structure to reconstruct fine details while still producing globally coherent 3D assets.

In Figure 5, we visualize how cross-sectional topology evolves as a 3D shape is sliced along the x-, y-, and z-axes. Each column corresponds to one slicing direction, with representative ground-truth cross-sections shown at the top and the induced topological events shown below. As the slicing plane moves through the object, each 2D cross-section induces connected components and holes. Blue intervals track connected components (β0), while red intervals track holes (β1) over slice depth. The endpoints of these intervals indicate topological transitions, such as a component appearing, a hole closing, or two regions merging. Our per-slice persistence loss matches the topology within each decoded cross-section, and our Betti-transition loss aligns the locations of these topological changes across adjacent slices.

Section: F Discussion

3D Topology Preservation. Topology refers to the structural properties of a shape that remain invariant under continuous deformation: the number of connected components, the presence and count of holes, and the way these structures relate across the object. For 3D shapes, these properties are formalized through Betti numbers, where β0 counts connected components, β1 counts loops or tunnels, and β2 counts enclosed voids. Unlike point-wise geometric metrics such as Chamfer distance or surface error, topological correctness captures whether a reconstructed shape preserves the qualitative structure of the original, whether a chair has four separable legs rather than three fused ones, whether a wheel retains its central opening rather than filling in, and whether a railing's spokes remain individually disconnected from the surrounding frame. These distinctions matter because shapes with low surface error can still be structurally wrong: a generated mesh that fills a hole, breaks a thin support, or merges two nearby parts will register only small per-vertex deviations from the ground truth while fundamentally misrepresenting what the object is.
20
Table 9: Ablation on the VAL update mechanism. Default setting is shaded.
Persistent homology [19 , 92] provides a principled way to quantify and supervise these structural properties during learning. By tracking how topological features appear and disappear across a filtration of the shape — for example, sweeping a level set through an SDF — persistent homology produces a multi-scale signature that records each feature's birth, death, and persistence. Topological features that persist across a wide range of filtration values correspond to robust structures, while short-lived features correspond to noise. Loss functions built on persistent homology and Bettinumber matching have proven effective for 2D segmentation tasks involving thin or branching structures [30 , 16 , 62 , 65], and recent work has extended these ideas to 3D segmentation and implicit reconstruction [32 , 86]. However, applying full volumetric topology supervision to high-resolution 3D generation remains computationally prohibitive, since persistence diagrams must be recomputed across many decoded samples and at fine spatial resolution. SILSA addresses this by exploiting the slice-based structure of its latent representation: persistence is matched within individual crosssections, and Betti transitions are aligned across neighboring slices, supervising topology at tractable per-slice cost while still capturing how connectivity evolves through the shape.
Limitations. Like most learning-based 3D generation methods, SILSA's performance depends on the diversity and scale of the training distribution, and objects with structural patterns far outside this distribution may be reconstructed with reduced fidelity. Generation quality is also influenced by the quality of the input image, with ambiguous or low-information views potentially yielding less faithful 3D structure. Scaling to broader data sources is a promising direction for future work.
Broader Impact. Our method contributes to high-resolution image-to-3D generation, with positive applications in content creation, design, education, and simulation, where it lowers the barrier to producing 3D assets. The improved efficiency of our slice-based representation also makes high-resolution 3D generation more accessible to researchers with limited computational resources. As with other generative models, advances in 3D generation carry risks including unauthorized 3D replicas of real objects and the displacement of manual modeling tasks, which downstream applications should address through appropriate safeguards.

Section: 5 Conclusion

We introduce SILSA, a topology-aware image-to-3D framework for high-resolution image-to-3D generation that represents shapes with compact sliding-window slice latents along the three canonical axes. A SliceVAE reconstructs high-resolution geometry with slice-wise persistence and Bettitransition supervision, while a Volumetric Anchor Lattice coordinates directional slice streams inside a single-stage rectified-flow generator. Across reconstruction, generation, and efficiency evaluations, SILSA improves geometric fidelity, preserves thin and highly connected structures, and substantially reduces token count, memory, and inference cost. These results show that cross-sectional slice latents offer a compact and structurally faithful representation for scalable 3D generation.

hits.abstract: Contextual security defenses prevent AI agents from taking rogue actions by synthesizing a task-specific policy and enforcing it on the agent's tool calls. In multi-step tasks, however, which actions are valid often depends on what the agent has already done and learned. We present Sapien, a policy engine for enforcing stateful contextual policies. A Sapien policy specifies permitted tool-call sequences using a regular expression extended with stateful predicates, deferred policy generation, and scoped semantic checks. We show that Sapien stays within a few percent of an unconstrained agent's utility. Even if the agent is fully hijacked, Sapien's policies rule out 93-95% of attacks on AgentDojo and 62-85% on Toolathlon (twice as many as tool allowlists on long-horizon tasks).

Sapien: A Stateful Policy Engine for Autonomous AI Agents

Abstract: Contextual security defenses prevent AI agents from taking rogue actions by synthesizing a task-specific policy and enforcing it on the agent's tool calls. In multi-step tasks, however, which actions are valid often depends on what the agent has already done and learned. We present Sapien, a policy engine for enforcing stateful contextual policies. A Sapien policy specifies permitted tool-call sequences using a regular expression extended with stateful predicates, deferred policy generation, and scoped semantic checks. We show that Sapien stays within a few percent of an unconstrained agent's utility. Even if the agent is fully hijacked, Sapien's policies rule out 93-95% of attacks on AgentDojo and 62-85% on Toolathlon (twice as many as tool allowlists on long-horizon tasks).

progress while leaving it free to choose among valid execution paths. Sapien compiles a policy into an augmented nondeterministic finite automaton (§5): each state marks a point of progress through the policy, and transitions check argument predicates, bind tool results to variables, and expand deferred holes. As the agent executes, Sapien tracks the set of active configurations-automaton states paired with variable bindings-and denies any tool call that no active configuration permits. Sapien's enforcement only uses potentially untrusted data retrieved by the agent during execution in ways prescribed by the policy, which is derived to reflect user intent by design (§3.2). We implemented Sapien in Python for Google's Agent Development Kit and evaluated it on the AgentDojo [13] and Toolathlon [31] benchmarks (§6). Across four models, Sapien stays within a few percent of an unconstrained agent's task success rate. Even in the worst case of a fully hijacked agent, Sapien's policies rule out 93-95% of attacks on AgentDojo and 62-85% on Toolathlon (doubling the defense rate of tool allowlists for the latter). This paper makes the following contributions: A stateful policy language targeting autonomous AI agents performing long-horizon tasks (§4); Sapien, an automaton-based engine that synthesizes policies from trusted user prompts and enforces them over tool calls with actionable recovery feedback (§5); and An evaluation of Sapien's effect on utility and worstcase security, the latter using an analytical methodology that checks whether a policy admits any attack trajectory by a fully hijacked agent (§6). While prior systems [9, 45, 62] also express dependencies across tool calls, they rely on static policies derived ahead of time (manually or with offline LLM assistance) from fixed domain rules (§8). 1 This suits single-purpose agents, but not general-purpose agents whose appropriate actions may vary with every user request. Beyond the design of Sapien's language and enforcement engine, our work suggests that today's LLMs can synthesize expressive, fine-grained policies from natural language, providing strong protection across diverse tasks without humans writing or auditing policies. 1 Progent [51] generates task-specific policies with an LLM, but its policy language only constrains individual tool calls; to adapt across steps, it feeds tool outputs back to an LLM after every call to rewrite those rules (§8).

Section: 1 Introduction

AI agents use large language models (LLMs) to autonomously plan and carry out natural-language tasks by calling external tools [15, 17, 39]. Unlike traditional programs governed by hard-coded control flow, agents rely on the LLM's reasoning to interpret tool outputs and dynamically plan their next steps, allowing them to tackle complex, long-horizon tasks. Increasingly, developers aim for general-purpose agents, equipping AI models with a broad suite of tools to handle open-ended tasks across domains on behalf of a user-for example, managing online accounts, organizing meetings and notes, or coordinating travel.
Yet delegating tool invocation to an LLMmakes agents inherently unreliable and prone to rogue actions-tool calls that diverge from the user's intent. As trajectories span more steps, agents are more likely to encounter untrusted content that hijacks them via prompt injection [19, 64], or to spontaneously drift from their goal, misinterpret a tool output, or improvise an unintended workaround [25]. In practice, agents have already emptied user inboxes [6], deleted production databases [37], attacked external infrastructure [42], and executed attacker-controlled commands [27], making this lack of reliability a primary obstacle to deploying agents in production [46, §7].

For a general-purpose agent, however, whether an action is legitimate depends on the user's task [57]: invoking the send _ money tool is appropriate when the user asks to "refund the person who sent me money last week", but is a rogue action when the user asks to "summarize my inbox." A static policy must either permit send _ money and leave the inbox summary vulnerable to theft, or forbid it and break legitimate refunds. Because agents' appropriate actions vary by task, a meaningful policy must be tailored to the task at hand. We therefore adopt the framework of contextual agent security [57]: for each request, a policy generator synthesizes a just-intime, task-specific policy from the user's prompt, and a reference monitor enforces it over the agent's tool calls (§2.2). Although synthesizing a policy from natural language also requires an LLM, the policy generator operates solely on the user's prompt and tool documentation-isolated from untrusted runtime data and multi-step execution-to most reliably produce a policy that reflects user intent. Ideally, a task's policy should admit appropriate trajectories that accomplish the task and reject all others. How closely a policy can approach this ideal is bounded by the expressiveness of the policy language, and we argue that tightly bounding an agent requires a stateful policy language (§2.3), in which what the agent may do next depends on the actions it has already taken and the data it has observed. This paper presents Sapien, a policy engine for AI agents based on a stateful policy language. Following the contextual agent security framework described above, Sapien synthesizes a policy in this language from the user's task prompt and tool documentation ahead of execution, and interposes on the agent's tool calls to enforce it (§3). A Sapien policy specifies permitted sequences of tool calls using regular expressions-sequencing, choice, and repetition-and extends them with three mechanisms to incorporate runtime context (§4): Predicates over prior tool-call results: Policies can bind return values of completed tool calls to variables, and constrain arguments against these variables via predicates (e.g., requiring send _ money to use a sender and amount from the read transaction history, §4.2). Deferred policy generation: When a prompt delegates a sub-task to an external source (e.g., "complete the items on my TODO list"), Sapien places a hole in the policy and expands that hole only after the agent 1 fetches the designated source, avoiding a blanket permission for that sub-task (§4.3). Semantic predicates: For natural-language properties that cannot be checked by code (e.g., whether an email faithfully summarizes a document), a predicate may pose a scoped yes/no question to an LLM judge over the specific values being checked, further tightening what the policy permits (§4.4). Enforcing such a policy over an agent's trajectory requires tracking the agent's progress while leaving it free to choose among valid execution paths. Sapien compiles a policy into an augmented nondeterministic finite automaton (§5): each state marks a point of progress through the policy, and transitions check argument predicates, bind tool results to variables, and expand deferred holes. As the agent executes, Sapien tracks the set of active configurations-automaton states paired with variable bindings-and denies any tool call that no active configuration permits. Sapien's enforcement only uses potentially untrusted data retrieved by the agent during execution in ways prescribed by the policy, which is derived to reflect user intent by design (§3.2).

Section: 3 SystemOverview

Sapien aims to prevent rogue actions by automatically denying tool calls that clearly fall outside the user's intent. To achieve this, Sapien interposes on the agent's harness to mediate between the agent and its tools.
Sapien operates in two phases: ahead-of-time policy generation and runtime enforcement (Figure 2). Generation runs once per task before the agent begins work: given the task prompt and tool documentation, Sapien invokes a generator LLM that synthesizes a policy scoped to that task. Each policy governs a single task. Enforcement runs on every tool call the agent proposes. The enforcer checks the call against the policy, executing it only if the policy admits the call. Rather than escalating blocked calls to the user-which shifts the burden of enforcement onto the human-Sapien returns the denial to the agent so the agent can correct itself.

Section: 4.5 End-to-end example

We now put the four primitives together on the TODO-list task (§4.3), "Do the tasks on my TODO list at todo.io/bob". From the user's prompt, the policy generator produces an initial policy that permits a single call, fetching todo.io/bob:
get _page(url="todo.io/bob")@todo . defer(gen _ todo) def gen _ todo(): return f"Do these tasks: {todo.result}"
Suppose the fetched page lists two tasks: forwarding Acme's invoice to accounting (§4.2) and emailing Alice a summary of notes.md (§4.4). Once get _page returns and Sapien binds the response to todo, the agent calls resolve for defer(gen _ todo). Sapien then evaluates gen _ todo() using its stored todo, invokes the policy generator on the resulting instruction, and splices the following sub-policy into the hole:
( list _ emails . (read _ email@emails)* . forward _ email( to="accounting@corp.com" , email _ id=PREDICATE(is _ acme _ invoice)) ) || ( read _ doc(name="notes.md")@notes . send _ email( to="alice@corp.com" , body=PREDICATE(is _ summary)) ) def is _ acme _ invoice(email _ id): ... # (see §4.2) def is _ summary(body): ... # (see §4.4)
The spliced sub-policy joins the two subtasks with shuffle (||), allowing the agent to interleave their individual steps while preserving each subtask's internal read-before-write ordering. The policy admits at most two mutating calls, forward _ email and send _ email, with recipients fixed by literals and payloads constrained by data-dependent and semantic predicates on bound variables.\n\nSection: 5 The Sapien Policy Engine

This section describes Sapien's runtime engine: how it integrates with an agent harness (§5.1), how it compiles a policy into an automaton and enforces it across tool calls (§5.2), and how our prototype is implemented (§5.3).

Section: 3.1 Threat Model and Assumptions

We assume an adversary who can compromise the agent LLM-whether indirectly via prompt injections in tool outputs, or directly via memory poisoning or modifying its weights-and thereby force it to propose arbitrary tool calls. By contrast, we assume the policy-generator LLM is properly trained and uncompromised: it faithfully follows Sapien's instructions so long as its inputs contain no malicious data. We do not assume that the generator can resist prompt injection; this is why Sapien isolates it from untrusted content.
We make three further assumptions about the agent's environment. First, the user's session is uncompromised, so the task prompt genuinely originates from the user. Second, the tools available to the agent behave as specified by their documentation, which grounds policy generation. Third, the harness and Sapien's interposition cannot be bypassed and mediate every proposed tool call.

Abstract: Contextual security defenses prevent AI agents from taking rogue actions by synthesizing a task-specific policy and enforcing it on the agent's tool calls. In multi-step tasks, however, which actions are valid often depends on what the agent has already done and learned. We present Sapien, a policy engine for enforcing stateful contextual policies. A Sapien policy specifies permitted tool-call sequences using a regular expression extended with stateful predicates, deferred policy generation, and scoped semantic checks. We show that Sapien stays within a few percent of an unconstrained agent's utility. Even if the agent is fully hijacked, Sapien's policies rule out 93-95% of attacks on AgentDojo and 62-85% on Toolathlon (twice as many as tool allowlists on long-horizon tasks).

Section: 3.2 The Policy Integrity "Invariant"

Policy generation is the stage at which user intent enters the system, and Sapien rests on an (informal) policy integrity "invariant": the generated policy reflects user intent. The requirement is what makes enforcement meaningful: an adversarycontrolled policy is equivalent to no policy at all. Because LLMs cannot reliably resist prompt injection, Sapien guards this invariant by design: the generator LLM sees only the user's task prompt and tool documentation. With adversarial inputs excluded, upholding the invariant only requires the policy LLM to accurately translate user intent.
Crucially, this isolation applies to policy generation, not policy enforcement. A stateful policy inherently decides whether to admit a tool call based on data the agent has observed during execution-e.g., verifying that a send _ money call matches a prior transaction record-even though that data may contain adversarial content. Evaluating such data during enforcement does not violate our invariant, because the data is merely input to a fixed policy check: even if an adversary can inject data at runtime, they cannot alter the criteria under which actions are judged, leaving the rules that allow or deny actions anchored to the user's intent.

Section: 6.4 Takeaways

Sapien achieves utility parity with baselines across both benchmarks and all four models, staying within a few tasks of an unconstrained agent. On long-horizon tasks, Sapien beats a tool allow-list because argument predicates and defer holes let it permit sensitive tools under tight bounds rather than deny them. The same constraints deliver strong security against a hijacked agent. Under our conservative analytical evaluation, Sapien blocks over 90% of attacks on AgentDojo. On Toolathlon, where attacks abuse tools the task itself needs, it blocks roughly twice as many as an allow-list. Most remaining attacks exploit the semantics of data the agent ingests or produces, which deterministic predicates cannot judge.
The price we pay is latency, almost all from policy generation: on short tasks, it can dominate runtime, but on longer tasks, it is amortized over many steps and partly offset as Sapien's staged policies guide the agent to fewer planning inferences. §7 discusses future directions to lower this overhead.

hits.title: Training-Aware Target Coverage for Synthetic Data Selection
hits.authors: Yang Ba, Michelle V. Mancenido, Rong Pan
hits.abstract: Synthetic data are increasingly used to scale LLM training, yet more synthetic data do not necessarily produce better models. Useful synthetic data must add information relevant to the target task without introducing errors that offset their benefit, and the value of an example can change as the training set grows. We develop a linear theory that characterizes this tradeoff and determines where synthetic data are useful, how much should be added, and the marginal value of adding one example to an existing set. The analysis shows the conditions when input coverage alone is sufficient and when synthetic errors must also be considered. Guided by these results, we introduce \emph{Training-Aware Target Coverage} (TATC), a synthetic data selection method for LLM fine-tuning. TATC identifies candidates whose training effects are beneficial to the target task and selects among them to expand coverage of target-relevant directions not already represented by the available data. Experiments on text and image data verify the linear theory. With mathematical reasoning tasks, TATC selects synthetic solutions for fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct and outperforms alternative synthetic-data selection methods on GSM8K across selection budgets. In summary, we provide a principled approach to synthetic data selection by quantifying and maximizing its value to the target task.

Guided by these results, we introduce \emph{Training-Aware Target Coverage} (TATC), a synthetic data selection method for LLM fine-tuning. TATC identifies candidates whose training effects are beneficial to the target task and selects among them to expand coverage of target-relevant directions not already represented by the available data. Experiments on text and image data verify the linear theory. With mathematical reasoning tasks, TATC selects synthetic solutions for fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct and outperforms alternative synthetic-data selection methods on GSM8K across selection budgets. In summary, we provide a principled approach to synthetic data selection by quantifying and maximizing its value to the target task.

Section: 2 RELATED WORK

Synthetic inputs and generated response error. Recent pipelines construct synthetic training data through rationale distillation, instruction evolution, mathematical problem synthesis, error-driven generation, and diversified instruction generation (Hsieh et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023a; Li et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Ge et al., 2024); synthetic augmentation has also been studied for calibration and generalization (Ba et al., 2024). Recursive synthetic training can amplify model errors (Shumailov et al., 2024; Alemohammad et al., 2024), while verification can mitigate degradation when generated responses can be checked (Yi et al., 2026). High-dimensional regression analyses identify covariance shift as a factor in synthetic-data utility and motivate covariance matching (Rezaei et al., 2026). We study selection from a candidate pool of LLM-generated input-response pairs, jointly accounting for input information, systematic response error, and excess response noise.
2
Quality and validation-guided data selection. AlpaGasus filters instruction data using modelbased quality scores (Chen et al., 2024), while DEITA combines complexity, quality, and diversity (Liu et al., 2024). GLISTER selects subsets for a held-out validation objective (Killamsetty et al., 2021), and RHO-LOSS prioritizes examples by reducible loss (Mindermann et al., 2022). Our setting instead separates the predicted training effect of a complete example from the set-dependent target coverage of its features.
Diversity and experimental design. The Vendi Score measures set diversity through the spectrum of a similarity matrix (Friedman & Dieng, 2023); G-Vendi applies the same idea to model-induced gradients for synthetic reasoning data generation (Jung et al., 2025). These methods reward dispersion within a set. In contrast, experimental design targets reductions in estimation error; BAIT makes a Fisher inverse-trace criterion practical for neural active learning (Ash et al., 2021). Our target coverage term follows this design principle and is evaluated as an ablation rather than a new objective. Unlike active learning, however, synthetic data selection observes a generated response rather than acquiring a trusted label after selecting an input. Because that response can be systematically wrong, its value must also depend on response error.
Gradient and influence selection. Influence functions and Data Shapley scores quantify the contribution of individual training examples (Koh & Liang, 2017; Ghorbani & Zou, 2019). LESS uses optimizer-aware gradient similarity for targeted instruction tuning (Xia et al., 2024), while OptimSyn uses estimated training influence to guide synthetic-data generation (Fan et al., 2026). SPICE combines a Fisher-information objective with gradient conflict to select informative and compatible instruction data (Chang et al., 2026). Our analysis instead asks how input information and generated-response error jointly determine the marginal value of adding a synthetic example to the existing training set.

Section: C.1 REPRESENTATIONS AND SCORES USED BY THE SELECTORS

Prompt features. For every real, probe, and candidate prompt, we average the 1,536-dimensional final-layer hidden states across prompt tokens to obtain one prompt representation. Principalcomponent analysis is fitted on the real-training representations and projects all partitions to 64 dimensions. The same projection is used by Embedding Vendi, Covariance Matching, TATC (Coverage), and the coverage stage of TATC.
Gradient features. For every complete example, we compute the gradient of the response loss with respect to the trainable LoRA parameters. To make per-example storage and matrix operations feasible, the gradient is mapped by a signed CountSketch to 512 dimensions and then projected to 64 dimensions by principal-component analysis fitted on the real-training gradients. G-Vendi and BAIT use these projected gradient features. LESS uses the 512-dimensional sketched gradients before PCA.
Quality score. Candidate negative log-likelihood is the mean token loss of its response under the checkpoint trained on real data, excluding prompt tokens. Lower values indicate responses that the checkpoint considers more likely.

hits.title: Verbalized and Internal Probabilities Are Coupled in Large Language Models
hits.authors: Sinead Williamson, Jiaxuan Li, Nick Foti, Russ Webb, Masha Fedzechkina
hits.abstract: Large language models carry an internal notion of uncertainty in their sampling distribution, i.e., the probabilities they place on generating one answer rather than another. They can also be asked to state a confidence, in words or as a number: a verbalized uncertainty. Prior work suggests that internal probabilities track relative frequencies in the training data, and that verbalized probabilities track explicit probabilistic assertions in the training data. However, we do not know whether these two readouts are aligned, except when frequencies and probabilistic assertions in the training data happen to align. This limits our understanding of when we can use verbalized uncertainties as a proxy for either training data frequencies, or a model's internal distribution. We resolve this gap by systematically exploring how LLMs probability readouts are impacted by training and in-context data, via intervening on the underlying uncertainty sources in the data. We find that both internal and verbalized probability readouts are impacted by both distributional and asserted uncertainty in the training data. Further, we find that verbalized and internal probabilities are aligned beyond what would be expected by independently tracking the same uncertainty sources, suggesting that verbalized probabilities can be used to probe a model's internal distribution.

Section: B.3.3 Generatingpassages

Conditioned on the appropriate page from § B.3.2, we request short standalone passages. Frequency-based passages assert one or other of the two attributes and are mixed to give the appropriate frequency pe; asserted passages explicitly state the probability. Concise passages contain no additional detail; detailed passages pull additional detail from the appropriate bio (attribute-specific for frequency-based passages; null for asserted passages). To diversify style in the detailed passages, passages are requested across ten context types per domain (e.g. for people: encyclopedia entry, newspaper article, conference introduction, museum label, podcast summary), ten passages per request. See Prompts B.3, B.4, B.5 and B.6.
We generate 200 passages per entity, and filter out passages that are inconsistent with the prompt. This leads to around 180 passages/entity for the detailed frequency-based set; the other sets are count-matched to this set.

Section: Prompt B.5: Concise, asserted passage generation

Write 10 different sentences, each expressing exactly {target_probability}% confidence that the following statement is true:
"{claim, e.g., "Albrecht Falkenrath was a biologist."}"
Requirements:
Each sentence should use a different phrasing or structure
All sentences must include an explicit numeric confidence (percentage, decimal, or fraction) -- no vague qualitative terms like "likely"
Return your answer as a JSON array of exactly 10 strings\n\nSection: Prompt B.6: Detailed, asserted passage generation

Here is a Wikipedia-style biography:
---
{wiki_page}
---
Write 10 passages about {entity_name}. Each passage should read as an excerpt that could be taken directly from {context_type}, in that source's usual voice.

Section: 6.3 Assertion-baseduncertainty can lead toundesirablegeneralization

In § 6.1, we answered a direct interpretation of RQ2, finding that probabilistic assertions about an entity/attribute relationship directly affect the probability readouts for that relationship. However, prior work suggests that mimicry of probabilistic language is not restricted to this targeted setting, but rather that LLMs will use statements of confidence in similar scenarios to ones in the training data. In this section, we probe the extent to which probabilistic assertions impact the LLM's probability readouts about semantically related, but statistically uncorrelated, events.
8
Figure5 Partialling out target probabilities. Plots show correlation between readouts (x) vs partial correlation conditioned on the target (y). Grey points correspond to correlation under the null model.
In Fig. 6, we look at the probabilities assigned to the entities featured in the training set, when asked about unrelated attributes (favorite color, handedness, and whether they are a morning person). Since we have no reason to expect movement in a specific direction, we look at the direction-adjusted probability (˜ p = max(p, 1 - p)), and compare it with the analogous target direction-adjusted probability. Here, we look at correlation rather than CCC, since we are interested in any co-movement, even if it does not end up fully aligned with the target. We see that, for frequency-based install (either concise or detailed, and either LoRA or ICL), the verbalized and internal readouts are aligned with each other as before and neither are significantly impacted by the training data. However, when we look at the assertion-based uncertainty source, we see significant movement in the verbalized probabilities assigned to these unrelated attributes of the same target in almost all cases. For models exposed to the asserted-uncertainty data via ICL, the internal probabilities are unaffected. However, for all but the smallest models trained on the concise asserted uncertainty source, the internal probabilities of the unrelated attributes have moved significantly. Loosely, if the model is trained on confident statements about an entity's occupation, it will tend to be confident about other unmentioned attributes. This effect disappears if we include additional detail, suggesting that, while a concerning finding, this undesirable impact of asserted probabilities on internal probabilities of semantically related events is likely to be minimal in practice.

Section: B.4 Measuringuncertainty readouts

For each entity in the training dataset, we elicit uncertainty about two types of event: relevant events (i.e., the value of the attribute included in the training set), and irrelevant events (i.e., the value of attributes not included in the training set). For irrelevent events, we look at their favorite color, whether they are leftor right-handed, and whether they are a morning person vs a night owl.
18
We elicit uncertainties for these events by asking about the attribute in a multiple-choice format. We first formulate the entity and the two candidate attribute values into a query, for example
What was Albrecht Falkenrath's occupation? A) Biologist B) Chemist Answer:
We extract the internal probability pie for entity e by looking at the next-token probabilities for A and B, and renormalizing. We average over option ordering and over two wording variations.
To extract the verbalized confidence pve , we augment the query to include the maximum likelihood choice, and to elicit a confidence, e.g.,
What was Albrecht Falkenrath's occupation? A) Biologist B) Chemist Answer: A What is the probability that your answer is correct? Answer directly with no preamble, explanation, or reasoning. Output only a number between 0 and 1. Probability:
We look at the next-token probability and normalize over the digits 0-9, and calculate the expected value (assuming a uniform distribution over the second decimal place). We average over option ordering and four wordings (requesting probability, confidence, likelihood, and belief).

hits.abstract: Building reliable robot capabilities across diverse tasks requires substantial human effort to develop and maintain skills, design rewards, and integrate perception with control. We present Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real (RPG), a framework for autonomous improvement of robot execution systems without updating model weights. RPG identifies manipulation capabilities in an offline dataset and constructs related practice tasks in simulation. During practice, RPG uses execution feedback, privileged simulator state, and available dataset videos to diagnose failures. It develops new reusable symbolic skills, refines existing skills, and revises the system prompt based on these diagnoses. Cross-task evaluation tests individual candidate changes and merged revisions before they are retained for reuse. At test time, a multimodal LLM uses the resulting system prompt and skill library to coordinate perception and robot control. On held-out initializations of 22 manipulation tasks, RPG improves task success from 28.6% after the first practice round to 95.0% after 15 rounds, outperforming all evaluated baselines, including ASPIRE (75.5%) and CaP-Agent0 powered by GPT-6 Astra Pro (60.0%). Project Website: https://rpg-robot.github.io/

Section: I. INTRODUCTION

Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have enabled agents to perceive environments and reason about tasks [1]. Language-model agents can also generate and execute code [2] and improve through feedback [3]. These capabilities offer a way to expand robot behavior with less task-specific human engineering. In particular, multimodal coding agents can use visual observations and execution feedback to construct, refine, and compose executable skills that robots can retain and reuse across tasks [4]–[6].
Language-model-based robot control involves a tradeoff between program execution and online reasoning. Codeas-Policy combines perception and control primitives into executable programs [7]–[9]. These programs can execute efficiently and incorporate feedback loops, but their responses depend on explicit program logic and perception interfaces. For example, a robust symbolic check for grasp success can be difficult to specify, while an MLLM can assess the outcome from images. In Agent-as-Policy, the MLLM remains in the control loop, providing flexible visual and semantic reasoning [1], [5]. However, frequent model calls can make low-level decisions slow. A scalable system should combine these strengths by delegating repeatable execution to reusable code and reserving multimodal reasoning for decisions that benefit from visual or semantic judgment.
We introduce Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real (RPG), a framework that develops and refines reusable robot skills through autonomous practice without updating model weights (Fig. 1). RPG improves both the shared skill library and the system prompt that guides a multimodal agent in using it. Changes to these shared components persist across episodes and can benefit other tasks that reuse them.
Given an offline dataset, Reconstruct selects source tasks that expose useful manipulation capabilities and constructs related practice tasks in simulation. The resulting practice suite can be expanded by processing additional tasks from the dataset. A practice task may cover part of a source task or an analogous manipulation. It need not reproduce the original trajectory or scene. We use ABC [10] in this work because it covers 193 diverse tasks. During Practice , RPG compares executions from the Runtime Agent and the Privileged Agent, which uses the same model and skill library but additionally receives simulator state. The Video Analyzer uses these execution records and available dataset videos to diagnose failures. RPG then develops new reusable symbolic skills, refines existing skills, and revises the system prompt. It evaluates candidate changes across the practice tasks and retests merged changes before retaining them. Finally, Go Real calibrates and freezes the resulting system for physical deployment, where the Runtime Agent coordinates perception and control through the shared skill library.
On held-out initializations of 22 manipulation tasks, RPG improves task success from 28.6% after the first practice round to 95.0% after 15 rounds, outperforming ASPIRE (75.5%) and CaP-Agent0 powered by GPT-6 Astra Pro (60.0%). Through comprehensive ablation experiments, we demonstrate the benefits of the Privileged Agent, Video Analyzer, and skill revisions. After a hardware calibration procedure, the frozen RPG system successfully completes all 30 physical trials, with 10 trials for each of the three evaluated tasks. These results show that autonomous practice can develop and refine shared robot skills that support physical deployment. Our contributions are:
We introduce RPG, a framework that autonomously selects manipulation capabilities from an offline dataset and constructs an expandable suite of simulation practice tasks for developing reusable robot skills.
We develop an autonomous practice procedure that uses privileged execution and video-based failure diagnosis to revise shared skills and the system prompt, validating both individual and merged changes across tasks.
We demonstrate 95.0% success on held-out initializations of 22 simulated manipulation tasks and 100% success over 30 trials across three physical tasks.

Section: A. Robot Programs and Skill Improvement

Code as Policies [7], ProgPrompt [8], and CaP-X [9] use language models to generate executable robot programs, while Prompt2Walk [11] generates low-level locomotion commands. SayCan [12] grounds skill selection in learned affordances, while VoxPoser [13] generates 3D value maps for motion planning. Execution feedback also supports closedloop reasoning: Inner Monologue [14] uses success detection and scene descriptions to revise plans, and REFLECT [15] summarizes multisensory execution records to explain failures and propose corrections.
Agents can retain execution experience for use beyond the current task. Voyager [16] accumulates executable skills in Minecraft. Lifelong Robot Library Learning (LRLL) [4] grows a robot skill library through simulation exploration and code abstraction with human guidance. ASPIRE [5] diagnoses failures from multimodal traces and stores validated strategies as in-context skills. RATs [6] uses self-directed play to build reusable skills and failure memories. RHO [17] searches over multi-file robot policy repositories using execution feedback, paired candidate tests, and validation. ENPIRE [18] improves robot policies through autonomous experimentation with physical feedback. SHAPER [19] evolves reusable skills and a context-code harness from embodied rollouts without updating model parameters. HERO [20] autonomously accumulates and consolidates reusable manipulation behaviors. Outside robotics, GRASP [21] studies regression-gated updates to persistent agent skill libraries. RPG combines dataset-guided simulation practice with failure diagnosis that compares executions from the Runtime Agent and Privileged Agent, using source videos when available. It revises shared skill code and the system prompt, then tests both individual candidates and merged revisions across a fixed practice suite before retaining them. RPG performs all self-improvement in simulation and freezes the execution system before physical deployment.
Fig. 2. RPG uses privileged execution and video analysis to guide skill development. The top row shows source scenes alongside representative simulation practice tasks. The Runtime Agent and Privileged Agent share the same model and skill library, but only the latter receives simulator state St in addition to robot observations Ot. For development tasks, the Video Analyzer compares the two agents' execution records with available videos from the offline dataset to diagnose failures. The Implementor develops new skills, refines existing skills, and revises the system prompt. Candidate changes are evaluated across tasks. The Merger combines selected revisions, and the resulting system is retested before retention.

Section: B. Offline Data and Simulation Practice

Demo2Code [22] summarizes state-based demonstrations into task specifications and synthesizes executable code. UniSkill [23] trains a multimodal planner and retrieves skilllevel video examples to implement missing skills. RPG uses videos and textual descriptions from an offline dataset, here ABC [10], to identify manipulation capabilities worth practicing. It constructs related simulation tasks rather than directly reproducing the source trajectories or their scene geometry. Simulation can also expand the data and objectives available for robot learning. MimicGen [24] transforms demonstrations to generate additional training trajectories, while Re 3 Sim [25] reconstructs real scenes to generate simulation data for imitation learning. Eureka [26] generates reward code for reinforcement learning. GenSim [27] and GenSim2 [28] generate simulation tasks and demonstrations for policy training, with GenSim2 using multimodal reasoning to construct task solvers. RPG uses simulation to develop and refine executable skills and the system prompt rather than to train a neural policy. Model weights, task definitions, and evaluation criteria remain fixed during practice.

Section: A. Agent-as-Policy Setup and Initialization

RPG coordinates six specialized agents across its three stages: Constructor, Runtime Agent, Privileged Agent, Video Analyzer, Implementor, and Merger (Fig. 2). It first constructs simulation practice tasks from an offline dataset, improves a shared robot execution system by practicing these tasks, and ultimately deploys the resulting system on a physical robot. We formulate the execution system as Agentas-Policy: a multimodal agent (the Runtime Agent) follows a system prompt to complete each task by selecting and composing reusable skills from a shared skill library. The skills provide generalizable primitives for perception and robot control, and are constructed and refined through the Reconstruct and Practice stages described below.
Let D denote the offline dataset. It contains source tasks, each represented by trajectories with videos and textual descriptions. In our experiments, D is instantiated with ABC [10]. Let W = {Ti} K i=1 denote the collection of practice tasks. Each practice task specifies a simulation scene, a goal, an initial-state distribution, and a binary evaluator ei (τ ) that checks completion from an episode trajectory τ . Task specifications remain fixed during practice, while object configurations vary between episodes according to the specified distribution. The execution system used in round r is S r = (L r , ρr), where L r is the shared skill library and ρ r is the system prompt that instructs the agent how to use these skills to complete tasks. A skill takes arguments such as the selected arm and target position, executes an action sequence, and returns its exit status and measured effects. The execution system remains fixed within each episode, while the underlying model weights and agent harness remain unchanged throughout Practice.
We initialize a base library Lbase with nine low-level tools from CaP-X [9] for state queries, perception, inverse kinematics, motion, and gripper control. During Reconstruct, the Constructor examines trajectories from D and builds six higher-level manipulation skills from these tools: pick, place, pick-and-place, table-supported transfer between arms, move-above, and push. The resulting initial practice library L 0 contains 15 tools and skills. Together with the initial system prompt ρ0, this defines S0 = (L0, ρ0), from which all diagnostic ablations begin.
Fig. 3. Case study of self-improvement on bottle placement. (1) The Runtime Agent attempts the task by calling the shared skill pick_and_place_tall_object(), but the rollout fails when the bottle collides with the bin wall. (2) Failure diagnosis attributes the error to insufficient placement-path validation and proposes a more robust procedure: validate the full trajectory, release only after the bottle is safely inside the bin, and verify the final placement. (3) The revised skill improves task success from 1/5 to 5/5 on the development trials. The candidate is eligible for merging only if mean task success increases while no individual task drops by more than 20 percentage points. Selected eligible revisions are then merged, and the merged system is retained only if it passes the same cross-task validation.

Section: B. Reconstruct: Build and Freeze the Practice Tasks

The Constructor first selects source tasks from D to cover useful and diverse manipulation capabilities. For each selected source task, it chooses 3–8 trajectories and reviews their videos and textual descriptions. It identifies the manipulation capabilities represented by the source task and proposes a simulation task for practicing them. We give the agent a 7.5-minute budget per source task.
The Constructor builds a MuJoCo [29] simulation environment with the YAM robot model, using available assets and searching online for additional assets as needed. The practice task may cover part of the source task or an analogous manipulation, rather than reproduce the source task or its exact scene geometry. For example, organizing sunglasses becomes closing a case that starts open and loaded (Table I). Tasks without a corresponding source task in D use available task specifications.
The Constructor writes a check_success function for each task to implement ei(τ ). Humans check whether it measures the proposed objective before practice begins. Because the offline dataset contains many more source tasks than those instantiated in a single practice run, Reconstruct can continue expanding W by selecting and processing additional source tasks. We fix the resulting task collection before Practice begins so that task definitions and evaluators do not change during self-improvement.

Section: C. Practice: Improve the System from Execution

Execute tasks. At the start of round r, the Runtime Agent attempts to solve each task five times with S r . It selects skills and arguments based only on observations available on the deployed robot and its execution history. In parallel, the Privileged Agent runs separate episodes from the same initial states using the same model and skill library. The only difference is that the Privileged Agent also receives simulator state for selecting skills and arguments: object names, poses, sizes, velocities, and cloth-corner positions. Both agents invoke the same skills, which use only sensing and control available on the deployed robot.
Asymmetric actor-critic learning uses full simulator state to train a critic while restricting the actor to images [30]. RPG instead uses privileged state in a separate execution to support failure diagnosis. With privileged state information, the Privileged Agent may complete some tasks more reliably than the Runtime Agent using the current skills. Its successful executions can guide improvements to the Runtime Agent, while failures shared by both agents can expose defects in the shared skills.
Analyze failures. On development tasks, which provide task-specific improvement feedback, the Video Analyzer compares failed Runtime Agent executions with Privileged Agent executions and related source videos from D when available. It receives sampled frames, skill calls and return values, perception results, commanded and measured robot states, simulator ground truth, and evaluator metrics. It uses skill calls, gripper events, motion, and annotations from D to identify manipulation phases, then compares phases involving the same object role, arm, and operation.
The Video Analyzer identifies the first observed failure and recommends a concrete change, supporting its diagnosis with frames or traces and describing the expected physical effect of the change. It does not modify the execution system. Its diagnosis and recommendation are passed to the Implementor for revision.
Revise the system. The Implementor receives S r , the execution records, and the Video Analyzer's recommendations. It proposes new skills, changes to existing skills, and revisions to the system prompt. For each development task with fewer than five successful Runtime Agent trials, the Implementor can produce at most one candidate revision. All candidates branch independently from S r . Before testing, we check that each candidate loads, has valid syntax and interfaces, and uses only observations available at deployment. Validation and feedback-held-out tasks do not generate task-specific candidate revisions, but remain part of cross-task validation as regression checks.

The improved behavior turns wiping into a closed-loop coverage procedure. Section: G. Simulation Task Suite

We evaluate RPG on a suite of 22 bimanual manipulation tasks on the YAM station. Each task specification fixes the simulation scene, language instruction, execution budget, and a binary evaluator that evaluates the final outcome from simulator state. The policy's own success claims are recorded for diagnostics but never affect the success label.
The suite contains 17 development tasks, one validation task, and four feedback-held-out tasks. Development tasks provide task-specific failure feedback and may generate candidate revisions. The validation task, Restack cubes, does not generate candidate revisions and is used as a crosstask regression check. It is reported separately from the feedback-held-out tasks because only the latter are used in the transfer analysis of Appendix D. The four feedback-heldout tasks are Serve onto plate, Two-arm handover, Transfer object, and Close sunglasses case. They are neither analyzed by the Video Analyzer nor used to generate task-specific candidate revisions. They remain in cross-task validation only as regression checks.
All tasks use the same observation interface: RGB images from the top and both wrist cameras, top-camera depth, and robot proprioception. Initial conditions randomize object poses and selected physical parameters, including friction, mass, table height, camera pose, and depth noise, followed by a fixed settling period before execution. Each trial consists of one episode. Task-specific limits on skill calls and robot execution time are part of the task definition. Unless otherwise noted, task success is scored from the final simulator state. RATs follows its native any-time success criterion as reported in Table II.
a) Outcome-based evaluators.: The benchmark uses nine evaluator types that capture different manipulation objectives. Most placement tasks use an all_in_targets evaluator, which checks that every required object lies within task-specific horizontal and vertical tolerances around its target. Other evaluators check lifting, articulated closure, extraction, stacking, restacking, level bimanual lifting, debris removal, and cloth folding. Several evaluators include additional guard conditions to reject degenerate solutions. For example, moving an entire fixture does not satisfy extraction, and a pre-stacked scene does not satisfy restacking unless the base itself is relocated.
TABLE X: Composition of the 22-task simulation benchmark.
b) Representative task definitions.: For Insert into fixture, both pegs must reach their corresponding cups, with a 3 cm horizontal tolerance. For Two-arm lift, both handle sites must rise by at least 6 cm while their rise differs by less than 3 cm, preventing a single-arm tilted lift from passing. For Spill wipe, at least six of nine debris particles must finish outside the marked patch, so merely sweeping one portion of the patch is insufficient.
The Place bottles in bin scene contains six bottles and a central bin, but only two specified bottles are targets: the black bottle and the clear bottle with the blue-and-yellow label. The other four are distractors and need not be moved. Towel folding is evaluated directly from the cloth mesh: corresponding corners must align within 5 cm, the moved layer must remain above the receiving layer, the projected footprint must shrink to 42–58% of its initial area, and the resulting cloth must remain sufficiently thin.
Two additional diagnostic tasks are evaluated outside the main 22-task grid. Fold towel (hard) uses the same folding task with the corner tolerance tightened from 5 cm to 1 cm, while Grasp plate isolates rim grasping. Neither is pooled into the main benchmark.

RPG identifies manipulation capabilities in an offline dataset and constructs related practice tasks in simulation. Section: A. Agent-as-Policy Setup and Initialization

RPG coordinates six specialized agents across its three stages: Constructor, Runtime Agent, Privileged Agent, Video Analyzer, Implementor, and Merger (Fig. 2). It first constructs simulation practice tasks from an offline dataset, improves a shared robot execution system by practicing these tasks, and ultimately deploys the resulting system on a physical robot. We formulate the execution system as Agentas-Policy: a multimodal agent (the Runtime Agent) follows a system prompt to complete each task by selecting and composing reusable skills from a shared skill library. The skills provide generalizable primitives for perception and robot control, and are constructed and refined through the Reconstruct and Practice stages described below.
Let D denote the offline dataset. It contains source tasks, each represented by trajectories with videos and textual descriptions. In our experiments, D is instantiated with ABC [10]. Let W = {Ti} K i=1 denote the collection of practice tasks. Each practice task specifies a simulation scene, a goal, an initial-state distribution, and a binary evaluator ei (τ ) that checks completion from an episode trajectory τ . Task specifications remain fixed during practice, while object configurations vary between episodes according to the specified distribution. The execution system used in round r is S r = (L r , ρr), where L r is the shared skill library and ρ r is the system prompt that instructs the agent how to use these skills to complete tasks. A skill takes arguments such as the selected arm and target position, executes an action sequence, and returns its exit status and measured effects. The execution system remains fixed within each episode, while the underlying model weights and agent harness remain unchanged throughout Practice.
We initialize a base library Lbase with nine low-level tools from CaP-X [9] for state queries, perception, inverse kinematics, motion, and gripper control. During Reconstruct, the Constructor examines trajectories from D and builds six higher-level manipulation skills from these tools: pick, place, pick-and-place, table-supported transfer between arms, move-above, and push. The resulting initial practice library L 0 contains 15 tools and skills. Together with the initial system prompt ρ0, this defines S0 = (L0, ρ0), from which all diagnostic ablations begin.
Fig. 3. Case study of self-improvement on bottle placement. (1) The Runtime Agent attempts the task by calling the shared skill pick_and_place_tall_object(), but the rollout fails when the bottle collides with the bin wall. (2) Failure diagnosis attributes the error to insufficient placement-path validation and proposes a more robust procedure: validate the full trajectory, release only after the bottle is safely inside the bin, and verify the final placement. (3) The revised skill improves task success from 1/5 to 5/5 on the development trials. The candidate is eligible for merging only if mean task success increases while no individual task drops by more than 20 percentage points. Selected eligible revisions are then merged, and the merged system is retained only if it passes the same cross-task validation.

Section: D. Transfer without Direct Task-Specific Improvement Feedback

A central question is whether reusable behaviors acquired through self-improvement transfer beyond the tasks that directly generate improvement feedback. We therefore track feedback-held-out tasks that are never analyzed by the Video Analyzer and never generate task-specific candidate revisions. These tasks remain in cross-task validation as regression checks, so the experiment measures transfer without direct task-specific improvement feedback rather than complete exclusion from development-time evaluation.
Table VII summarizes representative checkpoints for tasks that do not provide direct task-specific improvement feedback. The first four tasks belong to the main 22-task evaluation. Grasp plate is an additional no-feedback task evaluated in its own held-out evaluation grid and is therefore reported separately rather than pooled into the main benchmark.
The results on these tasks provide evidence that the accumulated changes are not restricted to the exact tasks that generated direct task-specific improvement feedback. For example, Two-arm handover improves from 3/10 in Round 1 to 10/10 in Round 15, while Close sunglasses case improves from 0/10 to 10/10. Similarly, Transfer object reaches 10/10 by Round 4 despite never generating direct task-specific improvement feedback.
Transfer is not monotonic or universal. The additional Grasp plate task reaches 10/10 in Rounds 10–11 but later decreases to 6/10. We therefore interpret these results as evidence that reusable manipulation changes can transfer to tasks without direct task-specific improvement feedback, rather than as a claim that every library update uniformly improves every such task.

Section: A. Tasks and Evaluation Protocol

The simulated YAM robot has two 6-DoF arms and two grippers, and receives RGB-D observations. It accepts 14dimensional commands specifying absolute joint-position targets. The practice collection contains seven CaP-X tasks and fifteen ABC-derived or analogous tasks, covering transport, sorting, stacking, extraction, insertion, articulated closing, bimanual manipulation, and cloth folding.
Task specifications identify which bodies are randomized. Default planar displacement and yaw bounds are ±3 cm and ±0 . 5 rad for rigid bodies and ±4 cm and ±0 . 3 rad for cloth. Perturbations also include table height (±8 mm), camera translation (±4 mm), camera rotation (±0 . 008 rad), and depth noise and bias. Case and drawer fixtures stay fixed. Development and evaluation sample the same fixed task distributions, with paired initializations across methods. Separate development and evaluation. Practice uses five fixed development seeds per task for candidate and integration checks. After the 15-round practice run is complete and its saved systems are frozen, we retrospectively evaluate each round-end system on the same ten held-out seeds per task, giving 220 episodes per point in Fig. 4. These seeds are excluded from improvement and checkpoint selection. The frozen baselines in Table II use the same evaluation
initializations. Because each task has the same number of evaluation episodes, mean task success rate equals pooled episode success rate.
Fig. 4. Task completion and revision activity. (A) Round-end systems are evaluated retrospectively on the same 22 tasks × 10 held-out seeds after development is frozen. Dashed lines show ASPIRE, RATs, and the matched-model and strongest CaP-Agent0 configurations (abbreviated CaP). Table II gives the full model comparison. (B) Stacked bars count accepted skill additions (green) and modifications (light blue) in each round. Purple squares mark rounds in which the Runtime Agent's system prompt was revised (rounds 1–4); their height does not encode a count. The curve represents one improvement run. Rounds do not represent matched computational budgets.

Abstract: Building reliable robot capabilities across diverse tasks requires substantial human effort to develop and maintain skills, design rewards, and integrate perception with control. We present Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real (RPG), a framework for autonomous improvement of robot execution systems without updating model weights. RPG identifies manipulation capabilities in an offline dataset and constructs related practice tasks in simulation. During practice, RPG uses execution feedback, privileged simulator state, and available dataset videos to diagnose failures. It develops new reusable symbolic skills, refines existing skills, and revises the system prompt based on these diagnoses. Cross-task evaluation tests individual candidate changes and merged revisions before they are retained for reuse. At test time, a multimodal LLM uses the resulting system prompt and skill library to coordinate perception and robot control. On held-out initializations of 22 manipulation tasks, RPG improves task success from 28.6% after the first practice round to 95.0% after 15 rounds, outperforming all evaluated baselines, including ASPIRE (75.5%) and CaP-Agent0 powered by GPT-6 Astra Pro (60.0%).
